sections.text: Foreword You are holding the yearbook of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2016. In this annual overview, you will read about how the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises, and what happened on shore to make all of this possible. Prominent in 2016 was the provision of emergency assistance. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, particularly Haiti lay in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide aid and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the assistance could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy also showcased its best side in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea. The maintenance program for the Walrus-class submarines is well underway, and the maintenance of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was successfully completed. Personnel underwent many new trainings, courses, and participated in (international) exercises. During the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and several ships to introduce visitors to our work. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. sections.text: 18 19 Organizational Overviews Organizational Overviews Department of Finance and Control (F&C) Head: Captain (ktz) M.F.C.M. Spierings The tasks of the F&C department consist of supporting C-ZSK by providing preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice. Additionally, compiling the budget, establishing the expenditure program, executing financial management, as well as contributing to information provision through management and steering reports, are part of the responsibilities. Finally, the department prepares the cash forecast quarterly, which also includes proposed measures to remain within the financial frameworks. The expenditures by C-ZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than budgeted last year. This increase was largely caused by personnel expenditures and additional costs for readiness and maintenance. Furthermore, C-ZSK deployment, partly as a result of the involvement with the European Border and Coast Guard Agency Frontex and the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean, better known as EU Operation Sophia, accounted for a larger share of the BIV budget (Article 1, defense budget) this year. In response to the increasing pressure on the defense budget, an Interdepartmental Policy Investigation (IBO) was conducted this year into the readiness process. This particularly mapped and analyzed the costs of deployment and readiness of the amphibious transport ships (LPDs). It became clear that the extensive deployment was displacing the available resources for readiness for basic warfare tasks. Additionally, a significant portion of the costs incurred for deployment was not reimbursed through the BIV. The financial challenges this year were further exacerbated by a rising necessity to replace outdated systems or repair them more frequently due to delays in replacement investments. Furthermore, the available budget limited the possibilities to maintain logistical supplies, resulting in an increasing so-called logistical debt. This year, the study 'Policy Review Marine Study' was also published. The starting point for this was the namesake study from 2005, based on which the composition of the fleet changed drastically. The study revealed that despite the fact that not all investment plans had been realized, all financial expenditures and the subsequent decision-making proceeded in a controlled manner. Thus, there was no need for additional measures. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam facilitates the training of the local coast guard near Libya by British and German instructors, by providing hospitality on board with accommodation, meals, and prayer spaces.

Personnel and Organization The further elaboration of the first partial agreement was still pending in 2016, which hindered the job allocation process due to uncertainty about when a new service end system would be implemented. At the end of November, an interim arrangement was put into effect, allowing personnel with a retirement date in 2017 to choose to work longer for a period of up to two years, until the new system is implemented. Due to increasing personnel shortages and a high ambition level of the organization, it became increasingly difficult in 2016 to find suitable solutions for personnel issues and vacancies. By clearly prioritizing and, where necessary, holding even more intensive consultations with the relevant departments and units, suitable solutions were found. The task assignment of the respective unit was also regularly adjusted. Following the vision document prepared by the Defense Personnel & Organization Division (DPOD) regarding the further development of the HR functions within the organization, a Cougar helicopter conducts fast rope training with marines.

sections.text: 24 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Defense, a number of advisors from HR together with colleagues from other branches of the armed forces have considered the challenges faced by HR professionals in 2020. Based on their proposals, this will continue in 2017, focusing on strategic HR themes such as talent management, strategic workforce planning, further development of the HRM system (E-HRM), sustainable employability, the change agent, and the driver of social innovation. Career Guidance Career guidance involves aligning the wishes of personnel with the opportunities provided by the organization. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each position or once every three years. This conversation focuses on personal developments in the near future and in the (medium) long term. The personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor also pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not advance in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section consists of four military offices for the operational service groups, marines, technical service, logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2016, this section had 37 military positions and 1 civilian position, of which a total of two were temporary positions. During the past year, one temporary position at the Marine Career Guidance Office and Technical Service was made permanent in the formation. Additionally, during the course of this year, a second civilian career counselor for civilian personnel was appointed. These three new permanent positions are funded from the Motie-Van der Staaij (MvdS) funds. Various groups of personnel, such as junior officers and the middle management among non-commissioned officers, experienced shortages. Unlike the previous year, a decision was made to implement more differentiation in compensation. In 2016, the 'Technical Allowance' was introduced for the next three years, which means that technical personnel in the rank of corporal up to and including warrant officer will receive a retention bonus under certain conditions. The idea behind this is that a retention bonus over multiple years will have more effect than the usual one or two years. Furthermore, an excessive number of first lieutenants of marines and corporals of technical service should eventually fill the shortages in the next higher ranks. Another sub-project within P-continuity that took shape is the establishment of Subject Matter Experts for various career paths. Questionnaires were also compiled to collect data on irregular departures and dropouts in initial training. HR made every effort to contribute maximally to "Safety at and from the sea," by placing the right people with the right training in the right positions. Integration The Integration department consists of the offices of Strategy & Advice (S&A), Policy Planning & Budgeting (BPB), and Investments (INV). Office of Strategy & Advice The S&A Office supports the Commander of the Naval Forces (C-ZSK) in his role as maritime military advisor to the Commander of the Armed Forces and the Minister of Defense. In 2016, the decision was made to work within S&A in three teams: Policy team, Knowledge team, and International Military Cooperation (IMS) team. The Directorate of Materiel Maintenance (DMI) provides for the periodic and major maintenance of all vessels of the Royal Netherlands Navy. Here is a submarine of the Walrus class.

sections.text: 26 27 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Policy acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Defense Staff and the Executive Staff (Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important activities this year included efforts within the framework of the 'Development of the Armed Forces' (DOKM) concerning the strengthening and renewal of the armed forces. The Knowledge team delved into the 'new' domains of Hybrid Warfare, Cyber, and Space in 2016 and contributed to various follow-up assignments under DOKM, such as 'Information as a Weapon' and 'Information as an Enabler'. This team was also actively involved in the network of the foundation 'Netherlands Maritime Country' and the analysis of the inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The IMS team supports CZSK in its international contacts and collaborations in cooperation with the Defense Staff (IMS). In addition to preparations for regular meetings within the framework of Belgian-Dutch cooperation (BeNeSaM) and the Naval Steering Group (NSG) with Germany, a highlight in 2016 was the organization of the Channel Command (CHANCOM) meeting. The Policy Planning & Budgeting Office (BPB) The Planning Coordination & Integration section (PLINT) is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. Over the past year, PLINT, in close cooperation with Finance & Control (F&C), proposed integral measures to Consumer Products and Retail (CP&R) and All Risks (AR) to keep the realization in 2016 within the budgetary framework. Mid-year discussions were also held with the Executive Staff regarding this. As a result, the execution this year was managed. In drafting the business plan for 2017, the integral planning was further improved. The Group Leaders and CP&R were explicitly involved for the first time in determining the key multi-year objectives to be achieved and the necessary activities for that. The increased focus on the groups contributes to more product-oriented thinking and working within CZSK operations. The implementation of the MvdS measures was already in full swing, and the first personnel arrived in 2016. Regarding equipment, the additional MvdS budget was partly spent on re-supply. The desk note was replaced this year as input from the DOs in the Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB) process by the execution note. As a result of the internal planning process, issues such as logistical debt, obsolescence problems, and currency issues were raised. The additional funds for enhancing operational readiness in the 2017 budget will be used to address issues from the 2016 desk note. As part of the BPB office, the Programming section is responsible for the establishment of the Readiness Plan (GSP). This GSP forms the long-term plan of the CZSK and looks about ten years ahead. It serves as the basis for various sub-plans within the CZSK, including the Maintenance Plan of the DMI, the Operational Annual Plan of the DOPS, the filling plan of P&O, and the training plan of Royal Netherlands Navy Training (OKM). This year, the establishment proved to be a dynamic process, where all parties involved had to regularly adapt flexibly to rapidly changing environmental factors affecting both the GSP and the various sub-plans. Changes in the Maintenance Program for the Walrus class (IPW) are an example of this. Furthermore, 2016 was focused on creating 'contingency plans' in preparation for expected financial shortfalls. For the Mine (Counter Measures Vessels) Operational Sea Training (M(CMV)OST) section, 2016 was marked by the responsibility for planning and monitoring material exploitation, particularly in the context of further implementing the demand and supply management (VAM) organization and processes. Additionally, under the leadership of CDS/DAOG, work was done on drafting the Defense Exploitation Plan – Weapon Systems (DEP-W). Of course, there were also several material processes that required the 'magic oil' of the section. As a result of MvdS, the section was expanded at the end of the year with a new component that must coordinate the introduction of new or renewed equipment within CZSK. The Investment Bureau (INV) is responsible within CZSK for the planning and realization of the bandwidth budget allocated to the defense components from the Defense Investment Plan (DIP). The Bandwidth Investment Plan (BIP) used for this includes all bandwidth projects of the CZSK, with a five-year outlook. The year 2016 showed a slight overrealization of the budget. Again this year, the needs were greater than the allocated budget, and several large projects were postponed to 2017, including the Seamanship Trainer, the small autonomous underwater vehicles for mine countermeasures, and the practical pontoons for diving operations. In addition to the CZSK Needs Assessment Coordination Meeting and the Project Consultation with the procurement agencies, the purple Bandwidth Coordination Meeting was also intensified at the end of the year. Finally, this year, part of the bandwidth was reserved for innovative projects.

sections.text: 28 29 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Operations and Information Provision Head: Captain (ktz) R. de Korte The year 2016 presented a significant number of challenges for the Operations & Information Provision (BVIV) department. Both the IT landscape and operational management were in full swing. Following the approval obtained in 2015, the department began establishing the ERP Competence Center CZSK (EC3). This required reviewing job descriptions and subsequently going through recruitment processes. By December 31, 2016, the EC3 was ready and was eighty percent staffed. The department also began taking over activities from the Sea Chain program (responsible for the CZSK migration to SAP), which ended on July 1. The program started with the takeover of the U2SAP project, which is responsible for the migration of material logistics operations from ULTIMO to SAP. U2SAP proved to be a complex project in 2016 that required significant attention from both BVIV and the users. Part of the project was completed this year, while the remaining portion is to be completed in 2017. The projects Migration Mercuur and Karel Doorman also took place under the auspices of BVIV in 2016 and were completed. Additionally, BVIV took over the documentation and temporary personnel, including contracted staff, from the Sea Chain program. The management that the department exercises over the phasing out of legacy IT systems, whose functionalities are being taken over by ERP M&F, remains essential. By the end of the year, the dismantling of a cluster of these legacy IT systems, which have influenced the material logistics operations of the Royal Netherlands Navy for many years (such as VAS, SGA, VPA, BUVA, BBSKM, FIDOKM, MATRACS, POS), was completed. This allows the department to gain further experience with the challenges surrounding the phasing out of applications. This is necessary as the phasing out or rationalization of applications is receiving increasing attention within Defense. The impetus for this is the intended transition of Defense to a new IT that is better able to support future IT-supported operations and command management. Not only is the migration to the new IT facilitated when there are fewer applications; where possible, savings on operating costs also follow. This phasing out certainly impacts the CZSK. In 2016, the Defense-wide program Border-Extending IT (GrIT) was initiated, which is to ensure the new IT in the coming years. The above also influenced the interface that BVIV forms between the Defense IT provider, the Joint IV Command (JIVC), and the Executive Staff, where the IT budgets are allocated. A new method of managing IT activities was introduced from the Executive Staff, the project portfolio management (PPM). The department participated in this PPM and coordinated the CZSK interests in an overstretched IT landscape where capacity, knowledge, and expertise in IT are scarce. The needs statement for E-welfare (internet) on board ships, established in 2015, will be honored for 2017. The department began planning activities to implement this project. A pilot was also initiated to improve internet provision at the barracks in Den Helder. Additionally, in 2016, E-welfare (internet) was delivered for the Marine Corps. Medical and Personnel Care Medical Care Operational Medicine Medcell 2016 was a varied and changeable operational year. There were many changes regarding planned ships and types of deployment concerning the Operational Year Plan (OJP). Notably, there were missions in the Mediterranean related to the migrant flows to Europe. From January 2016, there was a Fast Raiding Interception & Special Forces Craft (FRISC). During the training of members of the Libyan Coast Guard by British and German forces, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam served as the 'mother ship'.

sections.text: 30 31 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations detachment present on the Greek island of Chios as part of FRONTEX. In preparation for this, considerations were made regarding the provision of good personnel care, including aftercare. Additionally, the FRISC (Fast Response Intervention Ship Command) operators received a brief supplementary medical training on dealing with drowning victims and hypothermia. In March, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel departed for the Aegean Sea as part of Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 (SNMG2). At that time, there were still significant migrant flows between Turkey and Greece, and there was a possibility of having to rescue drowning victims in the event of a SOLAS case, so a plan was developed in preparation for how to accommodate the migrants. This took into account medical aspects such as extra oxygen, medication, and a reception plan. There was considerable attention to the aspects of Hygiene Preventive Medicine (HPG). Infectious diseases, such as scabies and lice, are present among migrants, and good HPG measures could prevent this from being transmitted to the crew. An additional AMV (Medical Assistant) was also added to increase medical capacity. During its deployment in the Aegean Sea, the Van Amstel did not have to rescue any drowning victims. At the beginning of May, it became clear that the Van Amstel would also be deployed as part of FRONTEX in the Mediterranean Sea between Italy and Libya. Experiences from other ships in this area indicated that migrants often needed to be rescued from unseaworthy vessels. Reports from allied nations showed that there were many minors and pregnant women among the migrants. In preparation for FRONTEX, the reception plan for migrants was reviewed in detail regarding HPG and medical aspects. Given the potentially large number of migrants to be accommodated over 24 to 48 hours, the medical team was expanded to a total of two AMA (Medical Officers) and three AMV (Medical Assistants). Additional courses and internships in pediatrics and obstetrics were undertaken in preparation. A total of 1,057 migrants were accommodated. However, on June 16, a baby named Gelila was born on board the Van Amstel under the supervision of the medical team, bringing the total number of migrants to 1,058. From October 19 to November 26, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was deployed in the Mediterranean Sea as part of Operation Sophia. Libyan coast guard personnel who were also on board were trained during this deployment. Additionally, necessary preparations regarding HPG took place again before the deployment, and the medical team was once again expanded. During this deployment, no migrants were accommodated. The crew of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel cares for migrants during Operation FRONTEX.

sections.text: 32 33 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations In the second half of 2016, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter was deployed as the flagship of SNMG2 in the Aegean Sea with a German staff. During this period, the flow of migrants between Turkey and Greece decreased significantly; therefore, there was no expansion of the medical team. The LCF De Ruyter rescued two drowning individuals who were attempting to swim from Turkey to Greece. After several hours under medical observation, they were handed over to the Turkish coast guard. The ship's doctor was also the Medical Advisor (MEDAD) for the German staff. From August to December, Zr.Ms. Tromp was deployed as the flagship for the anti-piracy mission Atalanta near the Horn of Africa. The naval vessel was augmented with an Advanced Resuscitation Team (ART) for this purpose. Due to the duration of the deployment, three rotations of surgical teams from the IDR took place. The ship's doctor on the Tromp was also the MEDAD for the staff. The deployment of a 'West ship' remained unchanged. In January, Zr.Ms. Friesland returned from the West, after which Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën, Zr.Ms. Groningen, and Zr.Ms. Holland departed for the West. The Holland, together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, was deployed for emergency aid following a hurricane in Haiti. The Holland conducted many beach landings to distribute water and food supplies but did not provide medical support. From the Pelikaan, limited medical emergency assistance was provided in remote areas. Throughout the year, medical support was provided to the Vessel Protection Detachments (VPD) of the Marine Corps in the Indian Ocean by adding a Medical Assistant (AMV-er) to each VPD team. During the year, an ATG was on standby, including a Role 2 Afloat for 20 days NTM. The personnel for this were ready, and most of the equipment was also available. However, there was no budget to purchase the remaining materials. On Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, a crew member distracts a young migrant with a stuffed animal. A German Orion conducts a practice airdrop in the Indian Ocean alongside Zr.Ms. Tromp. The container dropped by parachute is recovered by the Nautical Service.

sections.text: Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations In 2016, a definitive separation became possible in the examination floor of the DMC and the physician floor. These had been in a status quo for years in execution and with much dynamism in the staffing and organization of Defense, and were due for renewal. Follow-up steps were taken for the creation of new diving tables. Research for operational deployment was continued. An example of this was the promotion trajectory of Drs. T.T. Wingelaar under Prof. Dr. R.A. van Hulst (Hyperbaric and Diving Medicine) at the AMC (former HDMC). Drs. Furthermore, the content of this support was reviewed, and preparations were made to have it evaluated in the following year. In 2016, much energy was invested in the further development of deep diving tables. However, these did not proceed at the last moment and were postponed to 2017. In 2016, the Social Medical Service (SMD) provided occupational health care and personnel guidance to approximately 300 outpatient and about 50 inpatient patients, as part of the reintegration policy C-ZSK. The clinical patients almost always have an injury or damage to the musculoskeletal system and are internally guided to achieve the high fitness level of their operational unit. Over the past year, the physical profile of marines was improved, and the sports guidance was adjusted accordingly. Patients who worked internally at the SMD could, after completing their sports guidance, take both the tests for the required fitness level and the required strength level corresponding to the physical profile of marines at their own unit. The Primary Health Care Company (EGB) started on April 4. The SMD was not part of this. The SMD provided, among other things, primary occupational health care to soldiers of CZSK who were absent for more than six weeks and were seconded to the SMD. Since occupational health care also formally falls under the responsibility of the EGB, this was realized for the medical personnel of SMD through a delegation. The SMD also followed the quality requirements of the EGB regarding occupational health care. Over the past year, contacts with the Reintegration Services Center (DCR) were intensified to establish clearer agreements between SMD and DCR. The SMD carried out the reintegration in the first track for the first 12 months itself on behalf of CZSK, while the other military branches transferred reintegration to DCR after six months of absence. Meetings were held at set times with DCR: during the bi-monthly Social Medical Consultation and at 6 and 12 months of absence. With the relocation in 2016, the SMD made further progress. The intended location and the buildings on site Aardenburg in Doorn were examined, including the identification of bottlenecks and shortcomings. In the last quarter of 2016, discussions were intensified to establish a program of requirements. The SMD also provided input for the new reintegration policy document for Defense. The new document clearly described the obligations under the 'Improvement of Gatekeeper Act' and the medical examination for fitness for service, as well as the procedures to be followed in cases of social employability limitations, dropout during initial training, and service-related conditions. The new reintegration policy document will be evaluated by the unions in 2017. Lieutenant Commander (kltz) diving physician D.A.A. Koch observes how a diver steps out of the decompression tank.

Dit zal bijdragen aan een betere voorbereiding van de studenten op hun toekomstige taken en verantwoordelijkheden.

Daarnaast zal er aandacht zijn voor de integratie van digitale leermiddelen en technologieën in het onderwijsaanbod.

Dit omvat het aanbieden van gerichte trainingen en opleidingen die aansluiten bij de behoeften van de organisatie en de persoonlijke ambities van de medewerkers.

The KMTO collaborates with Regional Training Centers (ROC) spread across the country, which provide the VeVa training, specializing in Mechatronics levels 2 and 3. The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROCs and receive their Practical Vocational Training (BPV) at the KMTO. In 2016, 110 VeVa students joined the KMTO. The instructors of the KMTO link the learning objectives of these students to tasks in the naval practice. For example, they sail with naval ships and/or assist with technical tasks. In addition to the new entrants, the KMTO provides education for the already serving technical personnel. Various employees follow various technical vocational and/or functional training courses at different times in their careers, both in groups and individually, ranging from one-day to long-term courses. Through international cooperation, the KMTO also trains foreign naval colleagues. For instance, twenty Italian colleagues attended the Submarine Escape Training at the KMTO, five Chilean naval personnel completed the Module Training M-Frigates MK emergency measures, six German students finished the MIRADOR training, and the Peruvian Navy was visited to undergo the mechanical lessons 'Maintenance Gun.' sections.text: 56 57 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Development, Innovation, and Projects In addition to the 'core business' of the KMTO, which is training students in technology, the school is working on its own development. For instance, KMTO personnel are being certified. Instructors and educational development teams are undergoing training at the Expertise Center for Defense Training (ECOD). Furthermore, the school is working on the development of training equipment and environments. In 2016, for example, a new practical training room was opened, where the KMTO provides practical training for handling submarine batteries. By conducting training in this practical room, students gain a realistic view of the practical work environment aboard a submarine. In 2016, the KMTO was also active in innovative projects and pilots, such as GPAL, the development of the VeVa learning pathway, and MBO4 'Distance Learning'. It is a simple app that facilitates 'learning in the workplace' using videos. The VeVa learning pathway being developed is intended to offer students a challenging program during their BPV (Vocational Practical Training). The assignments in the learning pathway are related to tasks aboard the ships. In this learning pathway, the KMTO can implement this in a structured, safe, long-term planable manner, fully linked to the qualification dossier and learning activities at school (ROC). The MBO4 'Distance Learning' pilot for the maintenance technician is an outsourced training program from ROC Kop van Noord-Holland, where students (corporals TD) can obtain their MBO4 Service Technician diploma from the workplace within a year. The new form of technical education, the Continuous Technical Learning Lines (DTL), was also a major project that occupied the staff of the school in 2016. The DTL are becoming increasingly known within the TD of the navy, and the changes in technical education are gradually becoming noticeable and felt within the organization. To effectively guide and support these changes, the KMTO launched the communication campaign 'DTL, Tell-Tell-Tell!'. In 2016, the school communicated intensively with all involved target groups, organizing information sessions and conducting (ship) visits. To support this, the Glossy DTL, 'Tell-Tell-Tell', was developed, which outlines all the facts about the new learning pathways. The implementation of the DTL is a long-term process, and the total transition will take considerable time. In addition to these projects, the KMTO is also looking at how the school's setup aligns with (new) education, how the training programs align with the newly organized TD (where no distinction is made between Platform and Sewaco), and how the guidance of students in learning at the workplace can be best achieved. In addition to ship visits and training conducted on board, the KMTO also regularly supports the training unit of the Seatraining Command in preparing naval vessels for mission-specific readiness, sailing readiness, and exercise readiness. Additionally, the school participated in recordings for the TV program Het Klokhuis. The so-called solar boat project was also continued. A new team with MBO3 Mechatronics students chose this project within the training, which culminates in participation in one or more solar boat races. In 2016, the students participated in two solar boat races: the Eneco Solar Boat Race NK 2016 in Akkrum (May 6 and 7), where the students achieved first place in the V20 class, and the Dutch Solar Challenge (from July 2 to 9), where the 'Fair Play Award' was won. Operations Directorate

The Operations Directorate is responsible for the planning, management, and support of the readiness and (mandated) deployment of operational units, in order to effectively guarantee maritime expeditionary capability.

Staff Group Netherlands Maritime Force (NLMARFOR) 
Commander (also Flag Officer Operational Service): Commander (cdr) R.A. Kramer, succeeded on May 19 by Commander (cdr) C.H. Boelema Robertus 
Deputy Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) E.B. Brust 

The Netherlands Maritime Force (NLMARFOR) consists of three staffs: the (operationally deployable) Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) and the two training staffs Marine Training Command (MTC) and Sea Train Command (STC).

Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) 
Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) L.G.J. van den Berg, succeeded by Captain (ktz) F.J.G. Lenssen 

The Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) is the deployable C2 element of NLMARFOR. The MBS has various forms of appearance. In order of complexity, these are Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG), Commander Task Group/Commander Task Force (CTG/CTF), and specific staff elements such as Mine Counter Measures – Tasking Authority (MCM-TA). As CATG, the MBS must be deployable within a readiness period of seven to – depending on the chosen organization – twenty days. In some cases, the MBS must be supplemented for deployment as CATG with pre-identified and (partially) trained personnel from the CZSK and other operational commands (OPCOs) (augmentees). 

The main task of the MBS is to plan, coordinate, prepare, and execute (inter)national joint exercises and operations in which single deployed units (operationally ready naval and/or marine units) operate together to maintain operational readiness. 

In 2016, the MBS was active in various forms, during which the following diverse exercises were conducted:

COLD RESPONSE (February 18 to March 16) 
Participation in Cold Response was for NLMARFOR focused on maintaining the amphibious capabilities of MBS during the NRF year. Exercises were conducted in the highest spectrum of violence under the most extreme winter conditions. COMNLMARFOR led an amphibious task group consisting of Dutch, British, and American marines, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, USS Fort McHenry, and two Cougar helicopters. During Cold Response, a CET-FIT period was conducted in the vicinity of Harstad, Norway, where participating units followed a fixed program to increase interoperability. During the tactical phase, two landings were executed at Namsos. Close cooperation was maintained with SNMG1 and Norwegian units to protect the Amphibious Task Group (ATG) during the preparation and execution of the landings.

TRUTHFUL SWORD (April 11 to 22) 
Truthful Sword 16 was a Command Post Exercise (CPX) that took place in Wildflecken, Germany. The exercise was the first milestone in the certification of 1 German/Netherlands Marine.

A delegation from the MBS staff supported the exercise by providing maritime liaisons for the 1 GNC staff and acting as the Maritime Component Command (MCC) response cell. ADELBORSTEN CRUISE DURING BALTOPS (May 23 to July 1) The annual Adelborsten Cruise coincided with the Baltic Operations exercise (BALTOPS) and had a binational character this year. The task group consisted, in addition to Zr.Ms. Luymes, Schiedam, and Zierikzee, of the Belgian supply ship BNS Godetia, which served as the flagship. The main objectives of the deployment were to train and motivate the adelborsten. Zr.Ms. Urania was additionally involved in the cruise to provide the cadets with sufficient practical experience in the form of sailing hours. A challenging program was created that included at-sea replenishment, man overboard drills, navigation exercises, and hoisting exercises using the Alouette III embarked on BNS Godetia. Port visits took place in the following order: Berga, Stockholm, Kiel, and Aalborg. These visits were a good opportunity for the training naval officers to become acquainted with the representative tasks that belong to the responsibilities of an officer. JOINT VENTURE 16 (June 27 to July 11) MBS participated together with participants from the United Kingdom, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Norway in the Joint Venture 2016 exercise of the Joint Expeditionary Forces Headquarters (JEF HQ) in Cornwall, United Kingdom. Joint Venture is the annual joint exercise of the UK at the operational level. The objective of JV16 was to declare the Standing Joint Forces Headquarters (SJFHQ) Initial Operating Capable (IOC) for the JEF 2018. JV16 is part of a series of joint exercises that ultimately lead to the Full Operating Capability (FOC) status of the JEF in 2018. The Dutch participation consisted of a six-person team from MBS led by DCOMNLMARFOR. The JEF is a multinational cooperative framework established at the instigation of the United Kingdom. This exists outside the existing organizations such as the EU Battle Group and NATO but can be used in the context of both multinational organizations. BOLD ALLIGATOR (August 15 to 27) The amphibious exercise Bold Alligator (BA) took place in Norfolk. This large-scale exercise served as a rehearsal for the actual execution in 2017. Eleven members of MBS, consisting of marines and fleet personnel, participated in this exercise. BA is a large-scale amphibious maneuver in an artificial (Gulf region) scenario on the east coast of the United States. In addition to a complete amphibious task group, consisting of three large amphibious platforms with a full brigade of marines (up to 18,000 personnel), a carrier strike group (7,500 personnel) also played a prominent role to emphasize the importance of the air component. The exercise included various spectrums of violence and was primarily intended to strengthen the integration between the American marines and fleet along with international coalition partners. The participation of CZSK was valuable for knowledge exchange, such as in conducting river operations. The US Navy is partially capable of clearing a large area of mines in a relatively short time; however, they lack the capacity to do this in shallow water. The Netherlands does have this capacity and knowledge in the form of Very Shallow Water (VSW) teams, which proved to be of great added value. NLMARFOR MCM Work Up 2016 (September 5 to October 7) The triennial Binational work-up program MCM Work Up 2016 was conducted by Zr.Ms. Snellius, Vlaardingen, Schiedam, Zierikzee, BNS Primula, and a NL REMUS/VSW team. The units were supported by EGUERMIN, MOST, and the Naval Mine Warfare Mission Support Center. The deployment began with MCM training in the Firth of Forth near Leith/Edinburgh, United Kingdom. After that, there were percentage clearance and detection trials near Den Helder. The primary objectives were to improve MCM proficiency and increase operational readiness. Zr.Ms. Zierikzee practiced the detection and destruction of mines during an MCM exercise.

sections.text: 70 71 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations EMERALD MOVE (September 21 to October 14) Near the Italian island of Sardinia, MBS participated in the exercise Emerald Move. A total of ten European countries, including France, Spain, and Great Britain, practiced for the European Amphibious Initiative. The aim of this initiative is to create a multinational amphibious unit that can be deployed anywhere, both in EU and NATO operations. This year, the exercise was led by Italy and focused on testing and improving cooperation between the different nationalities. The Dutch participation consisted of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, which had 117 marines on board for this purpose. The program included many different exercises and a so-called freeplay phase in which air strikes, submarine threats, and amphibious landings were practiced. ULTIMATE SWORD 16 (December 7 to 20) The Command Post Exercise (CPX) Ultimate Sword was, after Truthful Sword, the second building block for the development of 1 German/Netherlands Corps (1GNC) into a supported Joint Task Force Headquarters (Land) (JTF HQ(L)). A small team from MBS participated in the planning and execution of this exercise. This included the deployment phase in the early stage of a small joint land-heavy operation for the subsequent certification exercise Trident Jaguar 17. For 1GNC, NLMARFOR is the natural partner in the maritime domain to operate (bi-) nationally at Joint Task Force level. During the execution of the exercise at the NATO Joint Forces Training Centre (JFTC) in Bydgoszcz, Poland, the MBS team acted as Maritime Component Command (MCC) and as a maritime advisor within the Initial Command Element (ICE). The team demonstrated the potential of maritime and amphibious capabilities to support a land operation and also emphasized the importance of cooperation with commercial shipping through the Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) organization. NATO Response Force (NRF) COMNLMARFOR was responsible as Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG) for forming and preparing the Dutch Amphibious Task Group (ATG) as part of the CZSK contribution to the NRF for 2016. Throughout the year, the ATG was on 20 days notice-to-move. This year was designated as the standby year. The composition of the ATG varied each month. The maritime contribution consisted of one or more amphibious transport ships, a submarine, a mine countermeasure vessel, a LCF, an M-frigate, and a hydrographic survey vessel. The core of the landing force was formed by 2MCG, C-battery with 120mm mortars from the VUSTCO, a TL platoon with the weapon system Stinger from DGLC, and enablers from (M)EODD, CMI, VSW, MEIC, and a cyber element. A Role 2 capability was also provided within the ATG. SATG supplied the landing craft (3x LCU, 6x LCVP, and 4x FRISC) and ABU. 300SQN provided 2x AS-532 Cougar transport helicopters and 860SQN provided 1x NH-90. The ATG was capable of being deployed anywhere in the world as part of NRF16 within the entire spectrum of violence, for a continuous period of 30 days, within 20 days. The higher command (1-up) was fulfilled by UKMARFOR, which took on the role of MCC. The ATG was not activated during the standby year. The next ATG contribution as part of NRF is scheduled for 2020. Off the coast of Sardinia, the international exercise Emerald Move 2016 is taking place. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam and Dutch marines are also participating in this. An LCU is landing vehicles on the beach.

Warnaar The STC is primarily responsible for the singular preparation of Dutch and Belgian naval units and the Coast Guard Cutters in the Caribbean. It also provides support to the fleet and NATO allies. The STC consists of 6 departments: Large Surface Units, Submarine Service, MOST, Force Protection and Boarding Operations (FPBO), Weapon System Management (WSM GBW), and STC-Shore. Sixteen of them were ultimately declared operationally ready. During the operational cycles of the units, they were also monitored and corrected where necessary. A total of thirty readiness checks were conducted. During such a check, it was assessed whether the units still met the high standard established during their preparation trajectory. At three units, an assessment was made at the end of their operational term on how they were preparing for maintenance. The V&M bureau supported three ships in updating their risk inventory and evaluation. Sea Training Command: Submarine Service For both operational and training missions, a total of fourteen towed array coupling actions and recovery operations were carried out. Sea Training Command: Large Surface Units (GBW) In 2016, STC GBW prepared eleven ships to various levels over twenty sailing weeks. After successfully completing the Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST), Zr.Ms. De Ruyter was declared organically operationally ready on April 8 and was prepared for her role as flagship of SNMG2. There was also a continuation and completion of the training process for Zr.Ms. Rotterdam this year. Although it is customary for the SARC-5 and SARC-6 to be conducted by FOST, this was not feasible for Rotterdam. Therefore, it was decided to have the final part of the training process conducted by STC-GBW. This took place during the exercise Cold Response 2016. In the Norwegian fjords, under the leadership of COMNL-MARFOR and together with Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, an intensive training program was executed, after which Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was declared organically operationally ready. After the first regular training process of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was disrupted in the previous period by the first deployment during the Ebola mission off the coast of Africa, the training process could be continued this year. Since there was a high percentage of new personnel among the crew, it was decided to restart the training process entirely. From March 29 to April 4, the SARC-3 was successfully executed, and the sailing readiness status was confirmed. Unfortunately, propulsion problems then arose, causing the continuation of the training process to be canceled once again. After the necessary repairs and modifications, the training process will restart next year. 

Zr.Ms. Holland also underwent a different training process this past year after the ship, as the first Ocean-going Patrol Vessel (OPV), had undergone a lengthy maintenance period. The SARC-3 was successfully executed in early April, followed by the SARC-4 from May 30 to June 10. During this, Zr.Ms. Friesland served as a sparring partner, and Aarhus, Denmark, was visited in between. A successful completion resulted in the status of exercise ready. Propulsion problems then meant that the planned NOST period could not take place. Since Holland was scheduled as the last unit of the year to serve as a station ship in the West, a solution had to be found. This was found, after the propulsion repair, in an extensive two-week pre-deployment training, followed by additional support during the departure to the Caribbean regions. As a result, Holland was timely mission-specific ready for her task in the West. This year, the ship was preceded in the Caribbean by Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën and Zr.Ms. Groningen, both of which underwent the usual pre-deployment training during their departure. In addition to these three station ships, two other units were also mission-specifically prepared this year. Zr.Ms. Van Amstel underwent mission-specific pre-deployment training for SNMG2 and FRONTEX during her departure to the Mediterranean. Zr.Ms. Tromp was mission-specifically prepared for her role as flagship of the anti-piracy EU mission Atalanta during her departure to the Indian Ocean.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.41)
sections.text: 78 79 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate was it time for a well-deserved port visit. The second British port of the year, Liverpool, was visited. After a short visit, the Tromp returned to Den Helder for the sailing family day. Despite stormy weather, it was a successful day, where family and friends got a good impression of life and work aboard a naval ship. In June, the last trip before the summer leave was scheduled. Together with Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, the Tromp set course for Norway for a number of tactical missile launches. On the way to Norway, several internal exercises were conducted in preparation for deployment for operation Atalanta immediately after the summer leave. Upon arrival in Norway, she visited the port of Tromsø. After a successful port visit, where the sun never set, it was time to head to sea for a busy program. During the day, exercises were conducted in preparation for operation Atalanta, while at night the entire ship went to battle watch for the launches. During these days, two Standard Missiles 2 and four Evolved Seasparrow Missiles were fired from Zr.Ms. Tromp. After the exercises, the ship was honored with a visit from the God of the North Wind, Aurealis Boreas, due to crossing the Arctic Circle. The entire crew returned to Den Helder after being treated to a blue nose, herring, and a glass of seawater or gin. Of course, the Panama lock, as tradition dictates, was also given a blue color. Upon returning to Den Helder, summer leave was on the horizon. In the last days, there was a flurry of activity to load the final supplies for operation Atalanta and to prepare the ship for the command transfer. With a short ceremony on the helicopter deck and in the presence of the entire crew, Lieutenant Commander (kltz) K. Schipper took command of Zr.Ms. Tromp from Lieutenant Commander (kltz) F.J.G. Lenssen. After the ceremony, it was time for summer leave and the last weeks at home before the ship would set off again for five months. After three weeks of absence, the entire crew was present again for two days of preparations, after which the ship departed on Wednesday, July 20, towards Somalia to participate in the EU mission Atalanta. After departure, a pre-deployment training was first on the agenda, led by Seatraining Command, where the final details were ironed out. After two logistical stops in Valletta (Malta) and Souda Bay (Crete), where the international staff came aboard, it was time for the Suez Canal. After a smooth passage, course was set directly for Djibouti where the command transfer took place aboard FGS Bayern. After this, Zr.Ms. Tromp was officially the flagship of the EU mission Atalanta under Dutch command. During the exercise Mjoelner, Zr.Ms. Tromp (right) sails together with the Danish HDMS Niels Juel. Crew of Zr.Ms. Tromp bids farewell to family and friends before departing for Somalia for the anti-piracy mission Atalanta.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.42)
sections.text: 80 81 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate Commander (cdr) R.T. Luyckx. The course was set towards the Gulf of Aden for the first days in the operational area. During the mission, the ship largely operated off the coast of Somalia. With patrols close to the coast, the presence of the EU ships was further emphasized and a picture was built of the situation in the area. After nearly four weeks, a first port visit was made to Salalah, Oman. After a few relaxing days, it was time to conduct patrols in the eastern coastal areas of Somalia. If an interesting contact was observed in these areas, a Friendly Approach was initiated. In this process, the embarked Marines, along with the responsible Human Intelligence officer, would approach the boat in question in RHIBs to engage in conversation and gather information with the help of an interpreter. The second port visit was scheduled for Muscat, Oman. After a well-deserved port visit, other activities were also carried out at sea. For instance, Zr.Ms. Tromp checked many EU-sponsored buoys designed to attract fish. The mission commander, Commander (cdr) Luyckx, was also taken to various other units for visits regarding the approach to piracy in the Gulf of Aden. After two port visits to Oman, the next two visits were to two southern countries. First, Tanzania, where the ship spent six days in Dar es Salaam, and then Port Victoria in the Seychelles. As part of the anti-piracy mission Atalanta, Zr.Ms. Tromp provided training to the local coast guard during its port visit to Port Victoria. This training focused on local maritime capacity building, where local authorities were trained in various skills necessary for maritime law enforcement. The training was specifically tailored for the coast guard personnel of the African country, who participated with a team of nine on the helicopter deck of the Air Defense and Command Frigate. The training was conducted by the Enhanced Boarding Element (EBE) of the Marine Corps, which has been added to the frigate's crew for the current mission. The training included apprehending and searching a suspicious person, entering a space, and moving around a ship. The participants demonstrated a high level of performance and showed great enthusiasm and eagerness to learn. This combination ensured that the training was a success. The new skills contribute to enhancing the capabilities of the Seychelles coast guard to better ensure maritime safety in the future. Zr.Ms. De Ruyter Commander: Captain (ktz) W.S. Vooijs EMSD Zr.Ms. De Ruyter underwent an intensive training program during the first three months of 2016. This program consisted of the Safety And Readiness Check (SARC) 4 period, followed by a training period and finally the Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST) in southern Great Britain. During the NOST, the ship and its crew were tested to the limit by the staff of the Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST) of the Royal Navy. Zr.Ms. De Ruyter concluded the NOST with a 'very satisfactory' as the final assessment. Additionally, during this period, the ship provided assistance to a vessel in distress off the British coast. The vessel had lost propulsion and was towed to a safe location by Zr.Ms. De Ruyter in bad weather. After the NOST, a period of maintenance, training, and sea trials followed. In early June, De Ruyter departed for Norway. Here, the ship participated in the international exercise Mjoelner, operating in the highest spectrum of violence. During this exercise, the ship conducted various missile launches under operational conditions. Following this successful exercise, a port visit to Vlissingen took place. Onboard, the agreement between Defense and the municipality was established. The Technical Service has the important task of properly maintaining the missile launch systems of the ships.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.43)
sections.text: 82 83 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations Vlissingen and the Water Authority Scheldestromen signed for the site where the new barracks (Michiel Adriaanszoon de Ruyter Barracks) will be built. Just before the summer leave of 2016, the ship received the order to prepare for a deployment as flagship for SNMG2. After departure on August 21, a pre-deployment training was conducted, and the ship prepared for its task of conducting reconnaissance, monitoring, and surveillance activities in the Aegean Sea. These activities focused on increasing situational awareness to support national and international efforts to combat illegal human smuggling in this region. Additionally, the ship could also be deployed for other NATO tasks if necessary. Zr.Ms. De Ruyter also served as the command platform from which the SNMG2 task group was directed by an international NATO staff led by a German admiral. During this deployment, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter also rescued two severely hypothermic castaways who were attempting to swim to Europe. Furthermore, the working visit of His Majesty the King at sea on November 16 and 17 was a special moment for the ship and its crew. During the return journey to Den Helder, the crew celebrated Christmas at sea, and on December 30, they docked back in their home port. Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) E.C.W. Jansen In the period from January 10 to June 20, 2016, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën was deployed as the Station Ship Caribbean Area (SSCG). After departing from Den Helder, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën conducted a pre-deployment training under the leadership of COMNLSEATRAIN-Boarding Ops. The focus was on the integration of the embarked Belgian boarding unit, training and integration of the boarding team into ship operations, and the execution of a DISTEX (disaster relief exercise) in Aruba. During the deployment as SSCG, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën, in addition to engaging in so-called 'Public Relations activities', fulfilled the three main tasks of Defense. First, protecting the integrity of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The presence as SSCG directly contributed to this. Second, maintaining international law and stability. The operational highlights were the four drug seizures; a total of 5 ships, 26 suspects, and 1540 kg of drugs were detained and handed over. Lastly, supporting the civil local authorities. During a coast guard period, assistance was provided to a Venezuelan bark with technical problems, which was towed to Aruba. Patrols were conducted west of Sint Maarten following the escape of a prisoner. A successful period is reflected upon, during which extremely pleasant cooperation took place with the staff of CTG 4.4, staff KW, the USLEDET, the KW boarding teams, and the flying KW and US Navy units. Zr.Ms. Evertsen Commander: Lieutenant (ltz1) E. Keizer, from August 26 Lt. Commander (kltz) W.H. van Gemeren The first half of 2016 was spent by Zr.Ms. Evertsen in Designated Maintenance. During the maintenance, the crew and DMI worked hard to prepare the ship on time. This hard work was rewarded on July 15 with the successful completion of the Safety and Readiness Check 1 (SARC-1). With the achievement of this first milestone in the reactivation process, Evertsen exchanged the shipyard for the operational quay. After the summer leave, on August 15, the nearly entirely new crew gathered for training period 1. On August 26, Lt. Commander (kltz) W.H. van Gemeren took command of Zr.Ms. Evertsen. On September 27, SARC-2 was achieved, and after the successful completion of the 'Fast Cruise' on September 29, Evertsen received the green light from the Commander Sea Training Command (C-STC) to begin SARC-3. After a maintenance period of one and a half years, Zr.Ms. Evertsen departed on October 3 for sea to conduct SARC-3, a ten-day period during which various exercises were held under the leadership of C-STC in the areas of safe navigation, fire, and emergency response. This intensive training week concluded with sufficient results and the designation 'ready to sail'. A sailing period of a total of six weeks followed. During these six weeks, the Sailing Material Trials (VMBs), various Sensor Weapon and Command Systems (SEWACO) and platform systems were tested. One component of this was measuring the acoustic signature on the sound track at Hegerness, Norway. This trial was followed by a port visit to Bergen on October 21. During the VMBs, in the context of the 'boat trip', a group of about thirty first-year cadets participated on board. This fresh intake

sections.text: 84 85 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate The cadets were quickly familiarized by the crew with life on board a naval ship. On November 18, the VMBs were completed, and the crew began training period 2. From November 22 to 24, the Evertsen was moored in the heart of Amsterdam to facilitate the CHANCOM. This concerns the annual meeting of the Commanders of the Naval Forces of all navies affiliated with the Channel. This year's edition was chaired by our C-ZSK, Lieutenant General (ltgen) der mariniers Verkerk. The last weeks of 2016 were filled with further preparations for the training trajectory that would continue immediately after the winter leave with the Staff Sea Check and SARC-4. Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt Commander: cdt R.T. Luyckx, from June 16 kltz R. van Twuijver, from July 18 acting commander/executive officer kltz J. Veken During the first half of 2016, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt formed the amphibious task group of the NATO Response Force (NRF) together with other fleet and marine units, Special Operations Forces, and the NLMARFOR-Maritime Battle Staff. The NRF is on standby to respond quickly in case of conflicts or to provide humanitarian assistance. To ensure the amphibious operational capabilities for the NRF, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt participated in two major amphibious exercise scenarios during that period, namely Cold Response and BALTOPS. Cold Response began a decade ago as a peacekeeping/peace enforcing exercise but is increasingly taking on characteristics of a classic 'steel-on-steel training'. This is mainly due to the tense relationship with Russia. Amphibious warfare, or combat at the boundary of land and water, is one of the priorities of the Dutch navy and our NATO allies. It was therefore not surprising that between February 19 and March 5, dots appeared on the horizon between the fjords off the Norwegian coast. Upon approach, it became clear that it concerned Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, and the American USS Fort McHenry. Both small vessels, manned by American, British, and Dutch marines, as well as various helicopters filled with sea soldiers, took off from the warships to participate in this exercise. From both the air and the water, about 350 marines, equipped with mortars among other things, landed. They advanced towards the nearby Namsos to secure two strategically important bridges so that ground troops could push through. There was some enemy resistance, but the marines, with the help of air support from four Norwegian F-16s, maintained control and drove the opponent away. Thus, the mission of the amphibious task group was successful. During the BALTOPS exercise (June 6 to 16), the amphibious training opportunities in a multinational setting were extensively utilized. Together with the British HMS Ocean and the American USS Carter Hall, the Dutch LPD was assigned to an amphibious task group under American leadership. Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt had a Swedish-Finnish task group on board for the occasion, the Swedish-Finnish Amphibious Task Unit (SFATU). The Swedish battalion staff was supplemented with Finnish staff officers and a complete Finnish company. Additionally, a German platoon was accommodated in this company, which was a guest on board Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, as part of the cooperation between the Marine Corps and the German Seebataillon. From Sweden, five Combat Boats (CB90) were also embarked that were part of the SFATU. Furthermore, several Finnish vessels (Jurmo and Jehu) joined this boat group in the theater. Finally, the Netherlands added two Cougar helicopters from the Defense Helicopter Command to the exercise. May 24, Girls' Day on Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt.

Operations Directorate

The first days of the exercise were marked by the so-called Combat Enhancement Training and Force Integration Training (CET/FIT) phase off the coast of Finland. This consisted of platoon and company actions in the Finnish archipelago. The CET/FIT was supported by Swedish Saab fighter aircraft and British Apaches from HMS Ocean. After the handover of command and a well-deserved port visit in Kiel, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt prepared for the four-year maintenance (BO-2). Zr.Ms. Rotterdam
Commander: Captain (ktz) H.H. Liebregs

On February 15, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed for Norway for the exercise Cold Response. This trip was not only for the exercise but also for the Safety And Readiness Checks (SARC) 5 and 6. Normally, these SARCs are conducted in Great Britain under the leadership of the Flag Officer Sea Training. Due to various reasons, this was not possible, and it was now conducted under the leadership of the Dutch training authority Seatraining Command. After these training activities were successfully completed, the ship was declared operationally ready.

During Cold Response, several assaults were carried out in the fjords near Namsos together with Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt and USS Fort McHenry. Onboard our ship, a British-Dutch Marine unit was deployed with British landing craft Offshore Raiding Crafts (ORC) for various amphibious tasks. During the voyage, the ports of Harstad and Sunderland were visited. On April 11, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed for Rotterdam for the exercise Gatorex, where exercises were conducted with the Port of Rotterdam, the Rotterdam safety region, and the Special Intervention Service (DSI) to counter terrorist actions. On April 22, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam returned to the port of Den Helder.

As a ready duty ship, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam went to sea again on May 8 to escort a Russian frigate sailing through the North Sea. The planned exercise Wetfeet for the First Military Training of Marines that followed was therefore slightly shortened. From May 23 to June 3, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam participated in the large-scale Belgian evacuation exercise Stormtide together with 1 MCG, the Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG), Belgian Marine units, and a Belgian Zodiac detachment. During the exercise, Zeebrugge was visited. As a conclusion, a port visit to Antwerp was planned. After the port visit to Antwerp, on June 7 and 8, a Russian submarine was escorted in the North Sea.

From July 4 to 15, the exercise Certifex was conducted, during which a Raiding Squadron of the Marines was certified. Part of this Certifex included a boarding operation on a special target ship off the south coast of England, the MV Tristam. The summer leave was from week 30 to week 32. On August 26, the sailing family day took place, during which family members were brought onboard with landing craft and could enjoy various demonstrations.

Zr.Ms. Rotterdam participated in the World Port Days (WHD) in Rotterdam from September 1 to 4. The short sailing trip from Den Helder to Rotterdam was in celebration of the 25th anniversary of the Central Military Hospital. The official opening of the World Port Days took place on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. During the WHD, the ship was opened to many thousands of satisfied visitors. Onboard was a beautiful exhibition of various historical military vehicles from World War II from the Foundation '39-'45. Additionally, several members of Vessel Protection Detachments were decorated during a medal parade onboard.

On September 21, a longer journey began, consisting of the exercise Emerald Move, followed by the EU training mission Sophia. Emerald Move is a large-scale international exercise for the European Amphibious Initiative (EAI), during which units are trained in amphibious operations in a European context. The exercise was led by Italy and was conducted on land and in the waters around Sardinia. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was equipped for this with the staff of the second Marine battalion, 45-commando Z-coy, 21st Raiding Squadron, a unit of the Belgian light infantry Brigade, LCTU-1 of the SATG, and two Cougar helicopters from 300 SQN. During the exercise, the port of Cagliari was visited twice for 'rest and recreation'.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.46)
sections.text: Operations Directorate After the completion of the exercise Emerald Move, the EUNAVFORMED mission Sophia commenced, during which Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, together with ITS San Georgio, was tasked with providing a platform for training the Libyan Coast Guard. The training for 37 Libyan trainees was conducted on board by ten British marines, five German naval technicians, two Greek boarding specialists, and an English teacher. Additionally, we also had a Cultural Advisor from CLAS, a Defense imam, and two interpreters on board to assist and support the Libyan military personnel. During the mission, 300 SQN with a Cougar, the boat company, and several marines were present for support. On October 31, the Minister of Defense, Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert, along with the Chief of Defence, General T.A. Middendorp, visited Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. The Italian Force Commander also made regular visits on board. During the mission, the ports of Catania (Sicily), Valletta (Malta), Augusta (Sicily), and Palma (Mallorca) were visited. In Augusta, an ‘EU medal parade’ took place on board at the conclusion of the mission. On December 14, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was welcomed back by the home front in its home port of Den Helder. Shortly thereafter, the winter leave began. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman Commander: ktz P.F.M. Reesink, from February 10 ktz S.L. Schot The first half of 2016 was focused on preparations. After the leave, the ship was to become part of a NATO formation, with a trip to East Asia planned for 2018. However, 2016 turned out to be the year in which everything went differently than expected. On January 7, the preparation process began with SARC-1, the first step in the ‘sea acceptance and readiness check process’. From February 3 to 5, the ship visited Amsterdam. Here, Minister of Defense Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert and her German counterpart Ursula von der Leyen signed a ‘Letter of Intent’ and a ‘Technical Agreement’ for the joint use of the JSS by the German Navy and for intensifying cooperation between the Marine Corps and the German Sea Battalion. The return trip to Den Helder was combined with the annual sailing family day. Over 200 family members, friends, and civilian employees took the unique opportunity to get acquainted with the Royal Netherlands Navy's sailing operations. Ktz P.F.M. Reesink handed over command to ktz S.L. Schot on February 10. From February 29 to March 4, the crew successfully completed SARC-3, demonstrating their ability to safely operate the ship. In the following week, various weapon systems were tested, and the ship set course for Warnemünde, Germany, to conduct an exercise with the German Sea Battalion. On March 10, the main electric motor (HEM) failed due to an internal short circuit. Further investigation revealed that this malfunction was due to a design and construction flaw. This could not be repaired on board. The port and starboard HEM are identical and were therefore both removed from the ship and sent for repair to the manufacturer GE. As a result, the preparation process, the remaining sailing program, and thus the possible trip to East Asia were canceled. The subsequent long period in port was utilized as effectively as possible. A significant number of crew members supported other operational units by filling in and worked with temporary placements. The ship itself regularly served as a location for events, briefings, tours, and exercises. An example of this is the exercise conducted by the German Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK) on board the ship from June 27 to July 14. During this, the Karel Doorman functioned as a platform from which a SOF exercise was directed. From the ship, personnel departed. As part of the cooperation between the Netherlands and Germany, the Royal Netherlands Army leased tanks from the Bundeswehr. Two of these Panzers were loaded on board the Karel Doorman in Den Helder and were shipped to Amsterdam where the official contract signing took place.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.47)
sections.text: 90 91 Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate conducted exercises with three German CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopters and various small vessels, practicing all aspects involved in a maritime hostage situation. While awaiting the repair process of the electric motors, as much preparatory work as possible was done in the autumn to ensure the reinstallation of the motors would proceed as efficiently as possible. On December 16, the first motor arrived by inland shipping in Den Helder, and it was successfully reinstalled in the week before the Christmas leave. Zr.Ms. Van Amstel Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) D. van der Neut, from September 1 Lt. Commander (kltz) H.J.F. Toebast After returning from winter leave, the year began with a short maintenance period. On February 1, the ship left the port of Den Helder to set course for Norway for various assignments. Initially, underway material trials (VMBs) were conducted, which only took place partially due to weather conditions. After a port visit to Kristiansand, torpedo firing exercises were carried out. This was followed by a port visit to Bergen, after which the command training of the Submarine Service was supported. The last assignment of this trip, testing the Low Frequency Active Passive Sonar (LFAPS), was not carried out. The ship was recalled to Den Helder due to a possible earlier deployment in the NATO squadron SNMG2. On February 20, the ship was back in Den Helder, and preparations for the early departure began. On March 7, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel left Den Helder, this time heading south. During this departure, a pre-deployment training was conducted under the leadership of Seatraining Command. After departure, it was decided to actually add the ship early to SNMG2. After a short stop in Plymouth, the advance to the Mediterranean Sea began. On March 14, a CHOP was executed to SNMG2. A few days later, after a short logistical stop in Cagliari, the ship joined this group in the Aegean Sea for NATO operations in the context of the migrant crisis. This was a special period, but due to NATO's mandate, the ship did not actually detain migrants. Nor did the frigate participate in rescue operations. During this period, port visits were made to Piraeus, Thessaloniki, Izmir, Aksaz, Canakkale, and Souda. The Minister of Defence Hennis-Plasschaert visited the ship on April 11. On April 24, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel was visited by the State Secretary for Security and Justice Dr. K.H.D.M. Dijkhoff. On June 3, the ship transitioned from SNMG2 to FRONTEX. For this, the ship moved to the sea area between Italy and North Africa via a short stop in Catania. The deployment for FRONTEX lasted until July 4. During this period, more than 1000 migrants were rescued from unseaworthy vessels and taken on board. At one point, there were more than 440 migrants on board. During this period, a baby was also born on board. The girl was named Gelila. The migrants were disembarked in Trapani, Valletta, or Augusta. On June 8, C-ZSK Lieutenant General (ltgen) Verkerk visited the ship during the FRONTEX deployment. After a short port visit to Cagliari, the FRONTEX deployment ended, and the return journey began. A final port visit was made to Mallorca, instead of the planned Ibiza, after which the ship returned to the port of Den Helder on July 15. After returning from leave, the command transfer took place immediately. On September 1, kltz H.J.F. Toebast took command from kltz D. van der Neut. The following week, the ship set out again. Zr.Ms. Groningen Commander: kltz W.A. Hansen, from March 11 kltz H.M. Sinke Zr.Ms. Groningen and her crew began 2016 with a period of rest after returning from the anti-piracy mission Atalanta. Zr.Ms. Groningen was deployed there as the first Ocean Going Patrol Vessel to combat piracy in the Gulf of Aden. Also in 2016, Zr.Ms. Groningen awaited a first. The ship was scheduled to participate in the EU operation FRONTEX in the Mediterranean in May and June. FRONTEX ensures proper border control and aims to prevent illegal trade in goods, weapons, and people. Before the ship would depart for the Mediterranean, it first sailed towards the fjords of Norway. Here, exercises were conducted in an international context with various submarines aimed at training submarine commanders. In addition to conducting simulated attacks on the submarines, Zr.Ms. Groningen was deployed to retrieve practice torpedoes from the water. During this three-week journey, two port visits were made to the Norwegian port city of Bergen. The spring was marked by a significant personnel change. A significant portion of the crew that had participated in Atalanta had since taken on other roles and had therefore been relieved. On March 11, kltz W.A. Hansen was also relieved after a command of 3.5 years. Kltz H.M. Sinke took over command and would prepare the ship for participation in FRONTEX. Zr.Ms. Groningen would be the first major surface unit of the Dutch Navy to participate in FRONTEX. The ship's task was to patrol south of Italy to monitor migrant flows and, where necessary, to bring migrants to safety when they were in distress. However, the mission changed due to a new prioritization, into a counter-drug operation of four months in the Caribbean from June to September. In a short period, the ship and crew were prepared for their West deployment. Groningen departed on June 5 from Den Helder to sail towards the Caribbean via the Azores. For its mission, the ship was equipped with an NH-90 onboard helicopter with an accompanying flight crew. Additionally, a team of marines came on board, as well as team members from the Caribbean Coast Guard and the U.S. Coast Guard. Even before the ship entered its first Caribbean port, it intercepted four hundred kilograms of drugs. A day earlier, the naval ship inspected a distressed sailing boat, whose crew had already been brought to safety shortly before. It turned out to be a successful deployment, during which nearly three thousand kilograms of drugs were intercepted and two search and rescue operations were conducted. Upon returning to Den Helder, one of the two main propulsion engines of the ship exhibited a technical failure. This led to additional maintenance being required in the autumn.

sections.text: Operations Directorate Operations Directorate was scheduled to repair the propulsion system. A planned sailing period to train navigation officers was canceled. Dijkhuizen 2016 was primarily marked for Zr.Ms. Holland by the completion of the Named Maintenance and the successful execution of a training trajectory, followed by deployment in the Caribbean. In February, the ship completed the first phase of the training trajectory and could safely operate on board. The following period saw the ship gradually prepared for departure to sea. In March, the second phase of the training trajectory was completed, after which Zr.Ms. Holland set sail in April for the third phase: safe navigation. During this time, it also made a port visit to Antwerp. By early June, it completed the fourth phase, during which both safe navigation and operational deployment were tested, and a port visit to Oslo was made. At the end of June, Zr.Ms. Holland visited Amsterdam, where crew members welcomed their families on board for a sailing family day. During the training trajectory, a major defect occurred in the main propulsion diesel on the port side. During the months of July and August, this issue was repaired to ensure the ship was ready for deployment in the West. At the end of August, sea trials took place, and the ship was technically ready for departure. However, due to the repairs, Zr.Ms. Holland was unable to complete the final phase of its training trajectory as planned in July. This final phase still needed to be executed before the ship could cross the Atlantic Ocean. The patrol ship departed on September 4 for its deployment in the Caribbean. Due to the still-to-be-completed training trajectory, a pre-deployment training in British waters was successfully conducted. The ship received the stamp of 'deployment-ready' and thus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. During the crossing, it quickly became apparent that it would be a remarkable journey. Several tropical storms arose and had to be avoided. One storm developed into a fierce hurricane named Matthew. Zr.Ms. Holland reached the Caribbean almost at the same time that this hurricane struck Haiti. The crew rapidly prepared to provide hurricane relief to the heavily affected island. Together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, the ship transported 450 tons of aid supplies to the coastal areas of Haiti. During this deployment, the naval ship primarily focused on alleviating human suffering and laying a solid foundation for other aid organizations to build upon. After the deployment in Haiti, the patrol ship conducted over a month of coast guard operations in cooperation with the Coast Guard Caribbean Area. During this period, the naval ship intercepted a Venezuelan drug transport. Additionally, it played an important role in the ceremonial celebration of the 240th anniversary of the first international recognition of American independence by the Netherlands on Sint Eustatius. A fishing vessel in distress was also rescued and brought to safety, and Zr.Ms. Holland docked in Aruba. Marines stationed there embarked aid supplies, such as water and tents for Haiti.

During these three months of deployment, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen neutralized several old bombs and naval mines, making shipping in the Baltic Sea significantly safer. Both 13 and 22 RSQN, along with approximately 30 novices from other operational units (SATG, SSG, NLMARSOF, 2 MCG), completed the Mountain Movement and Survival Course (MMSC), Mountain Warfare Training (MWT), and a final exercise during this training.
