In 2016, this included the National Remembrance Day in Amsterdam, the parade in Wageningen, the large swearing-in ceremony at the KIM, Veterans Day in The Hague, the World Port Days in Rotterdam, and the wreath-laying at the Oostplein in Rotterdam. In conclusion, it was a busy year for 1MCG. With a focus on preparation and readiness, the staff and units of 1 MCG were deployed again Qua Patet Orbis. The high pace and numerous activities did place a heavy burden on the personnel, particularly in the supporting units that were already struggling with personnel shortages. 2nd Marine Combat Group Commander: ltkolmarns H.J. de Vries 2nd Marine Combat Group (2MCG) executed a large number of missions, just like in 2015. Personnel participated in the Capacity Building Mission Iraq (CBMI) to train Kurdish Peshmerga to fight against IS. sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.60)
sections.text: 116 117 Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate contributed to Atalanta and various Vessel Protection Detachments (VPD) for the protection of Dutch merchant shipping. In the Caribbean, 2MCG provided various Guard Teams (GT) for counter-drug operations and detachments were supplied to support local authorities in Sint Maarten. 2MCG also contributed to FRONTEX in the Mediterranean and provided a security team for the training of the Libyan Coast Guard during Operation Sophia. Throughout the year, 2MCG was on standby as the core of the ‘Landing Force’ for the NATO Response Force under the command of COMNLMARFOR. For the staff of 2MCG, two major exercises were scheduled. The first was the Joint Arctic Training (JAT), organized for the training of units from 1- and 2MCG, as part of the first training year. This was an exercise in which more than eight hundred military personnel participated, as large parts of 24 Combat Support Squadron (CS SQN) and 25 Reconnaissance Surveillance & Target Acquisition Squadron (RSTA SQN) were also involved. The JAT concluded with a final exercise at MCG level. Another major maneuver was the European Amphibious Initiative (EAI) exercise Emerald Move in Sardinia (Italy), where the MCG staff commanded a multinational squadron and utilized various landing craft and Cougar helicopters. 20 Combat Support Squadron (CSS SQN) began supporting the JAT in 2016. From two fixed locations and several field locations, the 20th enabled the achievement of 2MCG's objectives. Subsequently, the MARSOC CERTIFEX was supported. The chain was also supported again during the Close Quarter Battle Instructors-course (CQBI) and the Live Fire Special Operations Urban Terrain module. 20 CSS SQN also participated in Emerald Move and supported the Sniper Concentration of 25 RSTA SQN. Despite limited space in the program, the 20th was able to conduct its own training during Emerald Move. The 21 RSQN successfully completed its training year and was MARSOC-certified at the end of the first quarter. Subsequently, they, in combination with 23 RSQN, were deployed extensively. Both units provided various rotations for CBMI and the Marine detachment in Sint Maarten. Additionally, they also supplied the VPDs and an EBE on board Zr.Ms. Tromp. After the conclusion of Emerald Move, the 21st also provided a team for Operation Sophia. In the first quarter of 2016, 22 RSQN was dismantled and reformed after three years of being a unit. From April, it carried out the training year, including a Live Fire Tactical Training (LFTT) in Denmark and the Mountain Warfare Training (MWT) in Great Britain. Throughout the year, personnel from 23 RSQN, a large part of which was deployed together with the 21 RSQN, were utilized. In addition to CMBI, Sint Maarten, VPD, and EBE, they also provided a rotation to FRONTEX. Highlights of 2016 for the 24 CS SQN included participation in the JAT, where a complete Combined Arms Live Firing Exercise was conducted. In the second half of the year, a start was made with the new readiness system for Combat Support (CS), which also included the enlistment of several reservists within the unit. The period concluded with a shooting exercise in Bergen-Hohne (Germany) where defensive and offensive operations with live fire were conducted. In addition to these trainings, 24 CS SQN contributed to CBMI, EBE, and deployed a complete Guard Team on board Zr.Ms. Groningen. 25 RSTA SQN participated with all its units in the JAT and the associated Combined Arms Live Fire exercise in Blatind. A FST participated in the Joint Fires Exercise Jasco Blue, together with units from the USMC and Royal Marines. The Recce Sniper Troop conducted a Sniper Concentration Exercise in Curaçao. Additionally, a Mortar Troop participated as part of the Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (VJTF) in the international exercise Noble Mariner and in the VJTF exercise Silver Arrow. sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.61)
sections.text: 118 119 Directorate of Operations Directorate of Operations Netherlands Maritime Special Operation Force (NLMARSOF) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. van Nee 2016 showed a high operational tempo for NLMARSOF. Many exercises and frequent deployments took place at the team level, but despite this small scale, the workload was high. For the staff and logistical support of NLMARSOF, the preparation, guidance, and processing of these small-scale deployments differed little from large-scale deployments. For the majority of activities, the focus this year was primarily on one of the three main tasks of NLMARSOF, namely Military Assistance (MA). During the annual multinational exercise Flintlock, led by the US Special Operations Command Africa (SOCAFRICA), the Joint Special Operations Taskforce - Trans Sahara (JSOTF-TS) contributed to the Trans Sahara Counter Terrorism Partnership (TSCTP). The Netherlands has been participating in this initiative since 2017. This year, a combined team from NLMARSOF, MARSOC, and ATG was involved in training and educating Senegalese NAVYSOF and COFUMACO, the equivalent of MARSOC and ATG. This training for special units took place in the maritime border region of northern Senegal and Mauritania. In 2016, NLMARSOF also provided Military Assistance elsewhere on the African continent. Among other things, to African partner units during the multinational maritime exercise Cutlass Express, led by Naval Forces Africa (NAVAF), where the focus was again on providing training in and around East Mauritius. Additionally, NLMARSOF trained alongside Danish SOF colleagues sister units from Cameroon and Nigeria in Cameroon, as part of the also multinational exercise Obangame Express. Serious deployment for NLMARSOF took shape in 2016 by deploying operators and staff on a small scale together with the Korps Commando Troepen within the Combined Joint Special Operations Task Force Iraq (CJSOTF-I), at and from Baghdad International Airport. In this mission, the focus was also on Military Assistance. Iraqi sister units and staff were trained and prepared for the fight against Islamic State (IS). NLMARSOF also trained and tested its basic and specialized skills again this year. For practicing SOF skills in ‘mountain and arctic’ conditions, one team and staff participated in Cold Response 2016. This time, integrated cooperation took place with American colleagues from Seal Team 2 and Norwegian colleagues from MJK within SOTG-40. The Snipers of NLMARSOF were able to sharpen and practice their skills in Denmark during Falcon Eye in 2016. This year again showed that the connections with Denmark, particularly the Fromandskorpet (FMK), are strong and have been of great value to NLMARSOF for years. The training opportunities in Denmark have also increased over the years, in line with the further professionalization of the Danish SOF component. An example of this was exercise Nighthawk, which was led by a Danish SOCC and where NLMARSOF participated with a team within SOTG 1.1. Seabased Support Group Commander: Major (majmarns) S. Peters In the past year, various logistically complex matters took place. Because the other operational units had a more than full Operational Year Plan (OJP), combined with various 'serious deployments', this placed a corresponding strain on the necessary logistical support. Although smaller units often went out, more smaller exercises meant significantly more work for logistical support and command. Also, the essential NLMARSOF during the counter-terrorism exercise Port Defender.

sections.text: 120 121 Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate faced regular pressure in the execution of an exercise or the necessary maintenance of used materials. For some already scarce operational pool resources, this meant that they were less available for certain units. Additionally, progress was made in further optimizing operations supported by SAP. To apply SAP optimally, several adjustments were made in the setup. However, working with SAP remains specialist work, which places increasingly higher demands on the training level of the personnel. In terms of training, there were also various challenges regarding IATA, ADR, and munitions. Regulations require that certain tasks be performed by qualified personnel. This year, the Material Management Quality Monitor (MKM) was also conducted. The unit passed this assessment with flying colors and sees the MKM as an excellent supplementary tool for further optimizing operations, thereby providing even better support to the operational units. From the unit, several specialists were again deployed with other units for exercises and 'real operations' to support them worldwide in their specific specialties. This includes logistics and munitions management, armaments technicians, communications service, and automotive mechanics. Expert groups have been established for the potential new barracks in Vlissingen. All specialist knowledge has been consolidated in this project with the aim of creating a logistics operational complex that is maximally designed to support the units of the Corps of Marines operationally in the future. Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J.W. Scheltema This year was marked by the development of the unit. It was the first time that the intended development methodology was applied at SATG to an operational subunit. Before the summer leave, LCTU-1 was officially certified as operationally ready. The second half of 2016 was characterized for LCTU-1 by the international exercise Emerald Move and operation Sophia. Operational Deployment Just before the summer leave of 2016, it became known that Zr.Ms. Rotterdam might be deployed for the EU mission Sophia in the Mediterranean Sea. The focus of this mission would be on training the Libyan Coast Guard so that they could better control and limit the migration flows to Europe. After the summer leave, it was still unclear whether the mission would proceed and what the exact tasks of LCTU-1 would be. During the exercise Emerald Move 2016, it was announced that Sophia would take place, and from the exercise near Sardinia, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam sailed on to Sicily for the 'swop' to Sophia. The task of LCTU-1 was to provide the 'guard teams' together with personnel from 21 Rsqn and to act as hosts for the Libyan trainees. Additionally, LCTU-1 supported the British trainers in providing various vessels during the 'boarding' training. Sophia was a special mission for LCTU-1, as the task package did not consist of assignments for which marines are initially trained. Nevertheless, Sophia was an interesting and educational period for LCTU-1, during which the camaraderie within the unit was significantly strengthened. For the European exercise Emerald Move, the action was prepared on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam during a briefing with a model.

sections.text: Operations Directorate Operations Directorate Training and Exercises In the first period of 2016, LCTU-1 had not yet been formed and consisted of a staff with ABU (LCCT-Heavy). In addition to individual training, personnel from LCCT-Heavy participated in the Joint Arctic training. The reconnaissance element of the unit also supported the NLMARSOF exercise Flintlock in Senegal. After training its own TTPs during various support tasks such as Practical Training for Officer of the Marines (POTOM) and Amphibious Dagger, support was provided from Zr.Ms. Rotterdam in May and June to the exercise Stormtide, initiated by the Belgians. Due to poor weather conditions, not all amphibious aspects were addressed. After supporting the FINEX of the POTOM in Rotterdam, LCTU-1 embarked on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to support the MARSOC CERTIFEX of 11 Rsqn and to certify LCTU-1 to MARC-3. Also during this exercise, the weather conditions were not favorable, and improvisation was necessary to certify the amphibious ship-to-shore capability. Ultimately, this was successful on Bankert Boulevard in Vlissingen, and LCTU-1 was declared operationally ready by MTC. After the summer leave, LCTU-1 prepared for the exercise Emerald Move. This amphibious exercise at brigade level, held near Sardinia, was initiated by the European Amphibious Initiative (IAE/EAI). The emphasis during this exercise was on demonstrating European amphibious capability. Through various sub-exercises and a high degree of integration exercises with various international partners, Emerald Move proved to be of great value for the operational deployability of the unit. Both the staff, the vessels, the beach element, and the reconnaissance element received more than sufficient training in Emerald Move to be well-prepared for the EU mission Sophia. Second Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-2) In January, part of the personnel from LCTU-2 participated in winter training in Norway. Thirteen personnel members were awarded a cold weather badge. Subsequently, amphibious support was provided to the exercise Cold Response in the Norwegian coastal waters. The months of May, June, and July were filled with participation in various exercises such as Safeguard, EMMV, and MIO training for 11 RSQN. After the summer leave, the World Port Days in Rotterdam began, where support was provided with 2x LCVP and 3x FRISC. After this, LCTU-2 supported the 22 RSQN with MIO training. At the end of November, the staff and 2x LCVP and 3x FRISC went to Brown Alligator in Sweden. Here, a shooting training for SATG was completed. FRISC Squadron Operational Deployment After a short preparation, in January 2016, a unit of five personnel was added to the Border Security Team (BST). This is an interdepartmental team that assists the Greek Coast Guard in processing the flow of migrants from Turkey. This support was part of FRONTEX, the European agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders. The BST was a new Dutch concept, consisting of personnel from the Royal Marechaussee, port police, customs, and the Royal Netherlands Navy. In this successful concept, a FRISC was chosen to patrol the territorial border between Turkey and Greece. This enabled early detection of migrants. Ultimately, hundreds of boat migrants were rescued, and arrests were made of individuals suspected of human smuggling. During the exercise Brown Alligator, amphibious and infantry operations with live firing by marines were practiced.

The voyages took its boats and crews this year from the Mediterranean Sea to the Norwegian waters and back to the Atlantic Ocean. Naval Aviation Service (MLD) Group Leader: Commander (cdr) G.A. Polet. For the Naval Aviation Service, 2016 proved to be another dynamic year. International Cooperation International cooperation continued and yielded good results. For instance, the MOU for operational data exchange with partner countries was renewed, and analyses of the Belgian Vigile ESM system were conducted within the framework of BeNeSaM. Multinational cooperation also continued. The MWC participated in the NATO Maritime Operations Working Group in Istanbul, Turkey, the Maritime Integrated Air and Missile Defense Panel in Southampton, United Kingdom, and the International Tactical Working Group meeting of the NATO Seasparrow Project Office in Rota, Spain. Publications During 2016, the MWC produced several publications. Three experimental tactics were published in CZSK Green Papers, as well as a manual on avalanche danger. The functional instruction Military Operations in Extreme Conditions (MOX) was also published. Additionally, five MWC newsletters on various topics were released. Finally, a Working Paper on technical exploitation in the maritime domain was also published. Operational Data In 2016, the MWC provided operational data to operational units and staffs nearly ninety times. Furthermore, seven pre- and post-deployment briefings were conducted. Analysts were again active as seariders on board; primarily for data collection but also, upon request, for training. Additionally, analysts also functioned as instructors this year. The MWC conducted the Acoustic Consolidation Course and Radar Techniques and Operations training in 2016. Military Operations in Extreme Conditions (MOX) In 2016, the role of Single Service Manager for MOX for the entire Dutch armed forces was further developed. For this, the Joint Knowledge Center MOX (JKCMOX) participated in national and international consultation structures in the Mountain & Arctic domain, such as the International Snow Safety Workshop in the USA and the Mountain Training Initiative in Austria and the Netherlands. The JKCMOX also supported (inter)national exercises. Examples include the Joint Arctic training in Norway, the Cold Response exercise with CLAS 43rd BE in Norway, the advanced module Avalanche Safety in Switzerland, and the retraining of UK Mountain Leader to Mountain Leader Teacher. In the jungle domain, a Military Tracker Instructors (MTI) course and a Military Tracker training were conducted, as well as two Jungle Warfare Instructors courses. In the last course, three students from CLAS and three from the CZSK were trained. Additionally, under the supervision of the JKCMOX, a Ground Sign Awareness Instructors course was conducted. Through contributions to the various trainings, the JKCMOX achieved a better structure in the Instructor, Teacher, and Supervisor system and facilitated the exchange of more experience within the jungle domain among the armed forces components. This will enable military components in the future to conduct their own trainings and courses, while the JKCMOX will continue to ensure quality. Manaslu Expedition In 2016, a unit from the Marine Corps climbed one of the world's highest mountains, Manaslu (8,163 m) in Nepal. As climbing high mountains falls within the expertise of the JKCMOX, Mountain Leaders from the JKCMOX supported the expedition. In preparation, several mandatory risk-mitigating activities were established for all participants, such as mandatory participation in the Alpine project in 2015, a medical examination, avalanche cases, a week of team building, and a simulated altitude activity in the pressure chamber of the Center for Humans and Aviation (CML). The expedition was also meteorologically prepared in close collaboration with the Joint Meteorology Group. By reaching the summit on May 9, 2016, the Mountain Leaders of the Marine Corps made Dutch history 60 years after the first ascent: the first military expedition to a mountain higher than 8,000 meters.

sections.text: 132 133 Operations Directorate Hydrographic Service Chief Hydrographer: Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck In January, Chief Hydrographer Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck and Director of Data Acquisition and Analysis of Rijkswaterstaat V.N. Zeijlemaker signed the management statement of the Dutch Hydrographic Institute (NHI). This provided a new impetus for the collaboration between both organizations. In June, the biennial North Sea Hydrographic Conference (NSHC) took place in Dublin, Ireland. The Dutch Chief Hydrographer chaired this conference. Important themes included participation in European projects, establishing a common reference level for depths, and coordinating hydrographic survey activities. In September, the Steering Committee of the International Centre for ENC’s, which distributes ENCs on behalf of more than forty hydrographic services worldwide, met in Amsterdam. During this meeting, the Chief Hydrographer was elected as the chair of the Steering Committee. In December, the IHO Meso American & Caribbean Sea Hydrographic Conference (MACHC) took place in Belem, Brazil. Again, the Dutch Chief Hydrographer chaired the conference. Important topics discussed included the international alignment of nautical charts, promoting the 'blue economy' by making hydrographic data and products more accessible, Capacity Building, and Satellite Derived Bathymetry (SDB). The MACHC elected the Chief Hydrographer as the representative of the region in the new IHO Council, alongside Brazil. At the end of 2015, a Picture study was conducted by the Director of Operations CZSK. The results of the study were discussed in early 2016 with the Management Team and the Hydrography Works Council. Following these discussions, it was decided to hold 'Live Standdown' sessions for all HYD staff. These will take place in 2017. The Memorandum of Understanding with the Maritime Authority of Suriname expired in September. The ENCs and paper nautical charts of Surinamese waters are now published in co-production with the United Kingdom Hydrographic Office (UKHO). Military Hydrography & Meteorology and Oceanography (METOC) The Military Hydrography & Meteorology and Oceanography section is responsible for all hydrographic surveys and work in the field of Meteorology and Oceanography. Within this section, plans are made and conditions are created to continue delivering high-quality products in the future. For example, active collaboration is taking place in the replacement of various hydrographic equipment of the Hydrographic Survey Vessels (HOVs). In 2016, an increasing demand for the searider capacity of the Maritime Environmental Information Centre (MEIC) was also noted. The custom products, such as Environmental Briefing Dockets, are becoming increasingly better in quality. Units are increasingly recognizing the importance of good hydrographic and meteorological information during exercises. Hydrography The first month of 2016 was focused on maintenance of the propulsion system for Zr.Ms. Luymes, but maintenance was also carried out on the ship during the last three months. This time for the twelve-year maintenance. This maintenance will continue until March 2017. Zr.Ms. Snellius also underwent major maintenance on the propulsion system in February and March 2016. The Snellius was deployed in 2016 during Beneficial Archer, and Zr.Ms. Luymes participated in the Interaction between a driver of a FRISC and the men of the Hydrographic Service in the RHIB just off the coast of Haiti.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.69)
sections.text: Operations Directorate Operations Directorate Adelborsten Cruise. During these periods, the HOVs and their crews once again demonstrated their potential as a multifunctional deployable platform. Rapid Environmental Assessments (REAs) were conducted, exercise mines were laid for the MCM workup 2016, and the HOVs provided fuel to various minehunters in the fleet multiple times. In 2016, an HOV was ready to be deployed as part of the NRF. However, actual deployment was not necessary. Particularly due to the unplanned deployment of Zr.Ms. Luymes for the Adelborsten Cruise and due to failures from various defects, it was not possible to achieve the required hydrographic days for this year. A total of 187 hydrographic days were realized. Maritime Environmental Information Centre In the past year, the METOC and Hydro seariders participated in various training sessions, exercises, and operations: the HQ weeks aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, Cold Response, Joint Warrior, Emerald Move, BALTOPS, Sophia, SNMG1, and Atalanta (added to the international CTF465 staff). For most exercises, the METOC and Hydro seariders provided a joint contribution as part of the N2 NLMARFOR. During the Cold Response exercise, they mainly provided environmental data and customized products. Hydrographic deployment is not always possible as part of an exercise scenario, but during Emerald Move, several beaches south of Sardinia were mapped for amphibious landings. Outside of all exercises and operations, a recording campaign was conducted in the Caribbean in the fall of 2016 with personnel from the MEIC and the HOVs. The plan is to continue this in the coming years. The recording campaign was interrupted to support the Human Disaster Relief Operation Haiti after Hurricane Matthew. The hydrographic team and recording system were embarked on Zr.Ms. Holland to conduct hydrographic REA operations along the Haitian coast. The ports of Port-au-Prince, Miragoane, Jeremy, and Les Cayes were mapped with the new MHP2 survey package. The MEIC not only provided searider support. Many operations and exercises were supported with specific products, such as Environmental Briefing Dockets (EBD) and Additional Military Layers (AML). Additionally, several missions were supported with very specific information deliveries, including for the Harpoon Trials, the MCM Work-Up, the LFAPS trials, and Torpedo Firing eXercises (TFX) southwest of Great Britain. These missions required custom-made products that integrated as much information as possible to provide a complete picture of the prevailing conditions. Support and Capacity Building The Hydrographic Service was also able to provide support for hydrographic education in 2016, for example, by allowing students from the Ocean Technology (Hydrography) program at the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz to sail with HOVs. The REMUS course held in Ostend for the Defense Diving Group and the Mine Service also received support from a hydrographer this year. Equipment Just like in 2015, the management of hydrographic quality standards remained a continuous source of concern in 2016. Throughout 2016, the service continuously assisted the DMO and DMI organization in efforts to maintain the material condition of hydrographic and METOC equipment within CZSK according to the prevailing qualitative standards. In 2016, a new hydrographic network was established aboard the HOVs, including a data server with greater capacity, faster network connections, and new recording and processing PCs. With this modernization, fast data transfer and good data storage are guaranteed for the near future. For the first time in 2016, Ellipsoid Referenced Surveying (ERS) was used on the HOVs. With ERS, it is possible to reference the measured GPS antenna height to a Zr.Ms. Snellius.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.70)
sections.text:
Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate has accurately established an ellipsoidal reference surface. With the availability of the Ellipsoid-LAT difference surface, a result of research from Delft University of Technology, a direct link between GPS height and the LAT reduction surface is now possible. In this way, measured depths can be directly referenced to LAT, without the need for tide measurements. To enable the ERS technique, the latest GNSS techniques have also been utilized. With the use of new GNSS receivers and a correction signal, the Hydrographic Surveyors (HOV) now have a very precise positioning capability at the decimeter level. In 2016, the need to replace the current Side Scan Sonars with a new system was approved. This means that in 2017, the replacement of the current systems can begin. This replacement ensures object detection during hydrographic surveys for the near future and allows the ships to continue meeting the requirements of the International Hydrographic Organization.

Military Personnel Despite a tight personnel situation, the hydrographic and METOC personnel have been deployed multiple times for missions, training, and large exercises, see deployment MEIC (2.4). Their specialization and expertise are highly valuable and contribute significantly to the success of missions and exercises. Retaining this knowledge and expertise requires continuous attention, given the tight personnel situation combined with the limited training budget.

Civil Production In addition to regular production work, significant efforts were made in 2016 to complete the SHIP2 project. The topics Bathymetry and Spatial Data Infrastructures have been finalized. Additionally, the Civil Production section was closely involved in the preparations for ISO certification. Personnel were trained as internal auditors or contributed to the creation of process descriptions. Work was also done on a quality workbook, which describes work instructions. A total of 53 new ENC cells were published, along with 9 paper nautical charts for the corresponding area. Furthermore, a new edition of HP1 The Netherlands Coast Pilot was released, along with the annual editions of HP7, HP1D, HP33, and HP33D. In total, 462 "Notices to Mariners" were published. After reaching an agreement with Belgian colleagues on a more logical map layout of the joint surveying area around the Western Scheldt, these new products were prepared in 2016. Publication of these will follow in January 2017. In the context of IHO, participation occurred in the Hydrographic Standards and Services Committee (HSSC) and various related working groups: Nautical Cartography Working Group, Nautical Information Provision WG, Electronic Navigational Charts WG, and the S100 WG. A major focus is the development of standards for data exchange based on S100 (the Universal Hydrographic Data Model). Furthermore, the section was represented at the IC-ENC Technical Working Group in Taunton and held working meetings with colleagues from neighboring countries. One colleague also attended the CARIS world tour in Bologna, Italy. At the request of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, a staff member from the Service (the head of Data Management) participated in a working group under the Sub-Committee on Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue (NCSR) of the International Maritime Organization (IMO). This working group assessed proposals for routing measures submitted by IMO member states. The service participates as a subject matter expert.

Geodesy and Tides The Knowledge Center for Geodesy & Tides (KCG&G) provides expertise for the measurement processes and publications of the Hydrographic Service, as well as for other branches of Defense and the government. The geodetic expertise is applied at sea, where water levels are of great importance. Tide knowledge is linked to marine geodesy. An important application is determining the correct coordinate systems and enabling conversions between them. This concerns both horizontal and vertical references. The choice of a system affects the calculation of points, lines, and areas. Another application is providing geodetic and tide data for general use, such as calculating boundaries at sea and publishing tide predictions.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.71)
sections.text: Operations Directorate Operations Directorate Support Hydrographic Publications The KCG&G participated in the Data Quality Working Group (DQWG) from May 10 to 12 in the United States. The DQWG is a working group of the Hydrographic Services and Standards Committee (HSSC) of the IHO. The working group was responsible for developing a standard for representing the quality of hydrographic products. Additionally, the KCG&G participated in the Surface Current Working Group (SCWG) from April 25 to 29 in Niterói, Brazil. The SCWG is another working group of the HSSC. The goal of this working group was to develop a standard for the delivery and representation of surface currents. The standard to be developed is based on components of the S-100 product specifications. Finally, the KCG&G attended the S-121 Project Team (PT) meeting held from December 5 to 9 in New York, United States. The S-121 PT is a sub-team of the S-100 working group and develops the IHO S-121 Maritime Limits and Boundaries data model. Support Hydrographic Surveys The Hydrographic Service continued its research from 2015 to realize a Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) plane, allowing for direct reduction from Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) to Chart Datum. This plane – LAT2016 – has been put into production aboard the Hydrographic Survey Vessels of the CZSK. Other On January 7, 2016, the Chief of Hydrography signed the Management Statement for the collaboration between Rijkswaterstaat and the Royal Netherlands Navy. This Management Statement reaffirms the existing covenant from 1986. The agreements, roles, and responsibilities have thus been re-established. Hydrographic Information Provision and Management The Hydrographic IV & Management section also focused this year on maintaining the current hydrographic production system and activities related to the SHIP2 project. Following the recalibration of the SHIP2 project in early 2015, further development of several increments took place in 2016, namely: • Nautical Publications: Replacement of the largely manual process. • Bathymetry: Replacement of the current bathymetric database with Workflow support. • SDI: Adequate integration of HYD systems with supplying data sources and provision of own data (in the context of ‘compliance’ with INSPIRE (new European legislation and regulations)). The increments Bathymetry and SDI were ultimately completed and put into production in 2016. The increment Nautical Publications will be phased out under regular management. Since the SDI increment ultimately took less time than planned, an additional increment was initiated: Management Information. This increment has been completed as far as possible and offered for testing. Personnel from the Hydrographic Service aboard Zr.Ms. Holland are conducting a test off the coast of Aruba.

sections.text: 140 141 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations With the completion of the SHIP2 project on December 31, 2016, a clear milestone was reached in the further professionalization of the supporting IT for the Hydrographic Service. Subsequently, the further development and professionalization of its functional management within the Hydrographic Service began. In particular, supporting tools play an important role in this. In 2016, the section also contributed to the broad implementation of quality management across HYD in the context of ISO 9001. Certification for this is scheduled for early 2017. Furthermore, cooperation with JIVC was intensified, particularly regarding standard (office) automation. Additionally, the Hydrographic Service partially transitioned to Windows 7 and preparations began to transition to Windows 10. Finally, the section made significant efforts, with the help of the released operational funds for 2015 and 2016, to address the IT backlog within the Service. Clear progress has been made in this regard. Staff Group/Account Management Operational Units In December 2016, the Sales and Distribution module of SAP was added to the inventory management system. This simplified the invoicing process. Public Relations In 2016, the Service had a stand at the Boot Holland and HISWA trade fairs. Additionally, it participated in the World Port Days in Rotterdam, and various groups of interested parties visited the Service, where subject matter experts provided presentations. Quality Management The ISO 9001 quality management system was further developed and implemented in 2016. Risks and opportunities were identified and elaborated on per section and at the level of the Hydrographic Service. Work processes were also described, and a customer satisfaction survey was conducted. Several staff members became internal auditors, and the first audits were carried out. This part of Dutch territory has the lowest priority because it is the furthest from the coast (between 150 and 180 nautical miles northwest of Den Helder), deeper than the rest of the North Sea, and does not form a usual shipping route. This is Zr.Ms. Luymes.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.73)
sections.text: 142 143 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations areas therefore have earlier issues with unfavorable loading conditions, such as high seas. Poor weather conditions caused the ship to return. On February 7, the ship entered Den Helder again. On February 9, the A-crew departed to sea for loading operations, and then on February 13 sailed to Zeebrugge, Belgium. In Zeebrugge, it conducted a Continuation Training (CT) for a week to enhance the level and competence of the crew. The Belgian-Dutch MOST led and provided the training. During this period, maneuvering, navigation, and fire drills were conducted, among others. The training period lasted until Friday, February 19, and resulted in a Satisfactory rating. The ship was to continue its way to the operational area for the execution of loading operations; however, these could not proceed again due to poor weather conditions. Therefore, the ship docked again in Den Helder on Monday, February 22. The B-crew set sail that same Monday for two weeks of loading operations. During this period, an ash scattering at sea was conducted. A select group carried out the ceremony with attention and respect, and a minute of silence was observed. Photos of the ceremony were taken for the home front. After the period of loading operations, the B-crew returned to the port of Den Helder on March 7. On the same day, the A-crew departed for a week of loading operations. A week later, they briefly returned to Den Helder to pick up a new navtex, before resuming loading operations at sea. A navtex provides the ship with necessary navigational and meteorological information and is required to be present on the bridge. Due to the bad weather, not much loading was done, but they mainly waited in the area for better conditions. On Monday, March 21, the A-crew returned. With this, they also completed their last voyage on Zr.Ms. Luymes for 2016. That same Monday, the B-crew set sail to conduct loading and wreck contact research. During this, the found wrecks in the area were further and accurately examined to determine the least water depth. On March 26, a tide gauge buoy that had been laid the previous year was picked up. This buoy with a sensor on the bottom measures water levels. By measuring this for a period of months, an accurate tide measurement and prediction can be made. On Sunday, March 27, they docked again in Den Helder. Between Monday, April 4, and Wednesday, May 11, the B-crew conducted loading operations, during which a few days were planned to be in Den Helder. This period went quite efficiently as the weather was good and the ship performed well technically and hydrographically. During this period, a tide gauge buoy was also streamed, and wreck contact research was again on the agenda. On Tuesday, May 17, the ship departed to load until May 19. The short duration of this period was due to the fact that the ship unexpectedly had to participate in the Adelborsten Cruise. For this, the ship was prepared in a very short time for an intensive six-week voyage. This posed a considerable challenge that was taken on with much enthusiasm by the crew. On Monday, May 23, a large group of cadets embarked for the Adelborsten Cruise, and Zr.Ms. Luymes, with the B-crew, set course for Ostend. Throughout the entire cruise, a Weekly Practice Program (WPP) was maintained. Together with the Belgian ship BNS Godetia, they anchored on May 24 at Vlissingen. A day after anchoring, the ships advanced towards Ostend. Along the way, various exercises were conducted, including helicopter operations with the Allouette from BNS Godetia and towing and RAS approaches with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and the aforementioned Belgian ship. On Friday, May 27, they docked alongside BNS Godetia in Ostend, where a festive weekend, 'Oostende voor Anker', was taking place. The crew and the cadets were able to enjoy themselves here after an intensive first week of the cruise. Early on Sunday, May 29, the weekend came to an end, and they departed for Berga, Sweden. Along the way, the lock in Brunsbüttel had to be passed. The ship then sailed through the Nord-Ostsee Canal to the Holtenau lock near Kiel and then further into the Baltic Sea towards Berga. Along the way, various exercises were regularly conducted together with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and BNS Godetia, including a Force Protection exercise and an NBCD carousel on board the ships themselves. On Friday, June 3, they docked in Berga, a naval base in Sweden. This port was filled with ships participating in the large exercise BALTOPS. After a short port visit, they set sail again on Sunday, June 5, towards Stockholm. However, Zr.Ms. Luymes fell outside the BALTOPS program due to the sudden involvement in the cruise. Therefore, the ship organized its own program with various exercises.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.74)
sections.text: 144 145 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate including small caliber weapons firing, anchoring, and finally a barbecue. At the end of the week, there was participation in a large photex where Zr.Ms. Luymes was positioned directly behind the command ship USS Mount Whitney. After a beautiful approach through thousands of islands, on Saturday, June 11, it docked alongside BNS Godetia in Stockholm. On Monday, June 13, it was time to depart towards Kiel to merge with Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Zierikzee, and EML Tasuja, a ship from Estonia. This week also had many exercises planned, including a hoisting exercise with the Alouette from BNS Godetia, RAS approaches, and a maneuvering exercise with small vessels. On Thursday, June 16, it docked for Kieler Woche in the Tirpzhaven in Kiel with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee alongside. During the open days that weekend, the line for other ships turned out to be just a bit longer than for Zr.Ms. Luymes; apparently, a hydrographic ship is less interesting than the Chinese or Spanish frigate that was positioned in front of and behind the Dutch ship. On Monday, June 20, the ship departed from Kiel with new cadets on board. It immediately set course for the Little Belt to conduct navigation exercises. This area was perfect for this purpose due to the many visual entry and exit marks. On the way, a hoisting exercise was conducted with an NH90 from the Danish Coast Guard. At night, the Great Belt was crossed to then continue the route around the north through the Oresund towards Copenhagen. On Wednesday, a large shooting exercise was held with moving targets at a Danish shooting range. On Thursday, despite the rain, the barbecue could still take place. The following morning, Friday, June 24, it docked in Aalborg. After yet another last port of the cruise, the ship departed on Monday, June 27, for the final week with Den Helder as the end destination. On the way, Tromøysundet was visited for the photex. This beautiful area is located in a kind of fjord. After a rough journey across the North Sea characterized by bad weather and high waves, Den Helder was entered on Thursday, June 30. The sailing family day planned for the next day unfortunately had to be canceled due to the circumstances. This marked an early end to the Cadet Cruise. On July 15, the C crew departed for the first time with Zr.Ms. Luymes to sea for loading operations and wreck contact investigation. Halfway through the journey, from Friday, July 22, to Monday, July 25, Stavanger was visited for a routine port visit, after which it docked again in Den Helder on July 28. On Monday, August 1, the B crew departed for loading operations with a port visit to Aberdeen. On the way, a Russian vessel was escorted for a short period. Luymes was in Aberdeen from Thursday, August 11, to Sunday, August 14, for a routine port visit. After this port visit, the rest of the week was spent loading until the day of entry. On Monday, August 22, the C crew went to sea for loading operations until September 5. On September 5, the B crew departed for loading operations. This time, there were special guests on board, namely students from the Willem Barentsz college. These students from the Maritime School Terschelling study Hydrography, and for them, this was an excellent opportunity to experience real work on a Hydrographic platform. Halfway through the sailing period, the first group disembarked, and new students came on board. This boat transfer was conducted above Terschelling. On September 19, the ship docked in Den Helder. This was the last trip for the B crew on Zr.Ms. Luymes. The C crew manned the ship until the end of the year. On Monday, September 19, the C crew undocked the ship. During this period, loading operations were carried out, with a routine port visit to the British city of Middlesbrough in between, before entering Den Helder on Wednesday, September 28. On Monday, October 3, the C crew departed for the last loading days of the year. On Thursday, October 6, the ship arrived in Den Helder for major scheduled maintenance. The ship will remain here until early 2017. Zr.Ms. Snellius Commander: Lt. Commander (ltz1) F. van Schoonhoven, from January 13 Lt. Commander (ltz1) F.M. Veenstra, from April 4 Lt. Commander (ltz1) E.P.J. Baars, from October 3 Lt. Commander (ltz1) S.M. Duineveld The first months of the year were focused on maintenance for Zr.Ms. Snellius. Nevertheless, the C crew had the opportunity to conduct the first hydrographic days of 2016 from January 8 to 12. After that, the ship was under maintenance until March 18. The diesel-electric engines received their necessary 10,000-hour maintenance during this time. Immediately after this maintenance, the C crew headed to Vlissingen for navigation exercises. These exercises lasted until March 24. From Tuesday, March 29, the ship resumed loading operations. During this period, the A crew and C crew switched.

Baijard General Service In the autumn of 2016, the replacement of the distinctive weather radar atop building Albatros was completed. The information from this radar is used, among other things, for an accurate display of the rain radar. The new system is capable of distinguishing precipitation type and intensity even better. In 2016, charging stations for electric cars were installed and put into operation by the EDB in various parking areas throughout the MBDH. These can be used for a fee by both employees and visitors. sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.80)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance Following the transfer of the historical 'De Voorwerf' in 2015, on January 11, 2016, the strip along the Oosterdok with buildings 022, 023, 024, and 027 (E-wing) was transferred to the Rijksvastgoed Bedrijf. The Project Bureau Marine Terrein Amsterdam took over its management and will carry out the redevelopment of the area on behalf of the state and the municipality. On the same day, the Minister of Housing and the National Service Stef Blok and the Mayor of Amsterdam Eberhard van der Laan opened a bicycle and pedestrian bridge over the Dijksgracht. This command bridge provides a direct connection between Kattenburgerplein and the Dijksgracht. The staff had already moved into the Provoosthuis (building 015) in November 2015. Originally, this was to be for a maximum duration of 1 year, but the planned relocation to building 012 has been postponed and may take place at the end of 2017. In addition to the EU presidency and the evacuation and relocation issues, the reorganization of various defense components and the implementation of SAP for shore establishments also played an important role this year. The consequences of this were clearly noticeable, as the facility and logistical processes within Defense are still undergoing changes. Nevertheless, the establishment, together with local supporters such as DBBO, PARESTO, and FBD, once again demonstrated in 2016 what the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam can and means for CZSK, Defense, the city of Amsterdam, society, and of course this year also for the European Union. Two of the crew members of the MEA, MATR 1 OD S. Jansen and MATR 1 OD A. Meerman, risked their lives this winter to rescue a drowning person from the IJ. For this, they were awarded the Blue Honor Ribbon and a reward, respectively. Events in 2016 In the first half of 2016, only smaller events could take place due to support for the EU presidency. Although the event center was closed in the first half of the year, visitor numbers decreased, but less than expected. This was mainly due to more intensive use of other facilities. However, from the summer period, operations could resume at full capacity. The last four months of the year saw visitor numbers nearly the same as in previous years. The total number of visitors this year was 17,639, during 776 events. The Marine Etablissement Amsterdam is still one of the few defense locations with flexible large hall capacity. Its central location in the Netherlands, the city center of Amsterdam within walking distance, and proximity to international entry and exit points make the barracks an extremely suitable and unique location for discussion forums, symposia, and presentations within the international defense community. In addition to the Golf World Cup, we were responsible for various large NATO conferences and symposia, including the CHANCOM: the meeting of all NATO naval commanders from the area around the Channel and the North Sea. Furthermore, the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam was once again the host location for BeNeSaM discussions between the Belgian Command Council and the Dutch Admiralty Council. New this year was the shared use of the conference facilities by civil partners, introduced by the Project Bureau Marine Terrein Amsterdam. Accommodation This year, 15,845 reservations for Short-Term Accommodation were processed for activities on and around the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam. Port Visits The number of port visits remained nearly the same this year. The largest applicants continue to be the port and towing service Den Helder and DDG. In many cases, a port visit was made to Amsterdam as part of a transit, but also to a greater extent for deployment in support of national authorities. This year, several foreign visits also occurred. Entrance Europagebouw. The building is beautifully illuminated in colors.

sections.text: 160 161 Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance Naval Base Vlissingen (MKVLIS) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (ltz1) H.W.M. Veldhuizen In 2016, the main task of accommodating CZSK ship crews was not fulfilled. However, tasks shifted this year towards a more general-facilitating defense location. After Zr.Ms. Evertsen in 2015, there were no CZSK units for maintenance in Vlissingen, which caused the accommodation of ship crews to stagnate. As a result, the two core tasks for Naval Base Vlissingen consisted of logistical support for a large number of exercises for CZSK units and other military components, and collaborating and networking with government agencies and the business sector for the new barracks to be built in 2021. The closing date of Naval Base Vlissingen has been moved from July 1, 2017, to April 1, 2018. This year, various units were accommodated at the base for battlefield tours. Among others, the MAROST (Maritime Support) staff, the Middle Defense Education (MDV), various CLAS units, and the Royal Marines (UK) were guests. The VeVa training program set up its camp at MKVLIS for a week in mid-2016, and the Certifex of the Marine Corps took place here in June. Additionally, MKVLIS provided space for the CLAS exercise Falcon Autumn this fall, as well as various other brigades. For a DBBO training this fall, accommodation was offered at MKVLIS due to a shortage of lodging at airbase Woensdrecht. Besides providing accommodation and food, the base was frequently visited throughout the year for theme days from the Zeeland Safety Region and consortia Michiel Adriaanszoon de Ruyterkazerne (MARKAZ), DSI, meetings, reunions (former crew members, COM, AVOM, BNMO, BOSS), and receptions. It also provided logistical support for festivities for the anniversary year, such as the tenth edition of ‘Rescue Vlissingen’ held in the summer. Permanent office and other facilities were provided to the staff of Defense Suppliers Oversight from DMO, 30 National Reserve (NATRES) battalion A-company, and a support team from CLSK. Furthermore, there has been a good relationship with the police and fire department for many years. The latter trains our emergency response organization biannually as standard. Week 19 was characterized by peak activity, as various components and agencies made use of the facilities. For instance, two defense components, the German/Dutch specialist organization in ground-based air and missile defense, and the Belgian Defence College, organized a battlefield tour. Additionally, the Customs Harmony practiced for two days at the base for a tattoo, and the 17th Armored Infantry Battalion, with 120 personnel, stayed there in preparation for the CLAS days in Goes. On Thursday, May 12, an information meeting was organized by RVB/PO-MARKAZ for potential entrepreneurs in the forming consortia. Due to the new barracks being built, networking in the province of Zeeland increasingly became an important task. The Commander and the Head of Logistics attended the New Year's receptions of various municipalities in Walcheren. They also attended various commemorations and wreath-laying ceremonies, including the Remembrance of the Dead on May 4, commemorations in Kapelle, Vlissingen (Uncle Beach/Battle of the Scheldt), and Bergen op Zoom (Canadays). Furthermore, they attended the Zeeland Veterans Day, networking days of the Safety Region, the Prinsjesfestival, former contact days, and meetings of various institutions. The highlight was the awarding of the ‘Franklin D. Roosevelt Four Freedoms Award’ to German Chancellor Angela Merkel on April 21 in Middelburg. The closing date of the barracks was postponed in 2016. This is related to a delay in the realization of the new barracks, which is now scheduled for completion in 2021. On June 22, an important agreement was signed on board Zr.Ms. De Ruyter during a port visit to the city of Vlissingen. This agreement between the Ministry of Defense, the province of Zeeland, the municipality of Vlissingen, and the Water Board specifically concerned agreements regarding the territory. During the nighttime exercise LOWLANDS 2016, a Medevac Cougar picked up "wounded" in Vlissingen.

Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) drs. J.P.S.M. de Rooij After a longer period without a First Officer, the new officer took office at the beginning of January. After an intensive onboarding period, the foundation was laid for the continuation of the path that had been set. There were many personnel changes, partly due to the expiration of regular placement periods. Crucial in this was the change of the Head of Logistics, a position that was not filled again for several months. A budget was made available for this, which, supplemented by a planned maintenance budget, was expected to lead to extensive renovation. The execution of this was postponed from 2016 to 2017. Furthermore, the kitchens that had already been tendered in the barracks were completed just before the summer. The tendering of the second series also started, which was ultimately delivered in December. This led to a significant improvement in the barracks facilities. A long-running project, the armory, was brought back to the required security level after the summer. This had some impact on operations. Due to the increase in personnel, there was an additional need for storage, as well as for office and workspaces. With minor adjustments, this need could be met. However, for the storage issue, it was necessary to resort to Maartensdijk. In terms of maintenance, the outdated condition of the barracks continued to take its toll. The KKW shooting range also experienced significant wear problems, making it unavailable for shooting training for several months. Due to the increase in equipment and personnel in the barracks, certain operational activities were more or less forced to relocate to Maartensdijk. With this relocation and expansion, the last location increasingly became a stronghold of storage and transshipment activities and maintenance, leading to operational risks. During an IL&T inspection in August, covering both the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks and Maartensdijk, several minor deficiencies were identified. Fortunately, these could be quickly remedied. Nevertheless, due to the results of the inspection in Den Helder, all of CZSK was placed under intensified supervision. Main building of the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks, Doorn.

sections.text: Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Due to the numerous terrorist attacks in Europe in 2016, security measures were significantly tightened. This had an effect on the Defense Security and Surveillance Organization (DBBO) and the security officers at the barracks. The sports hall proved to be a risky object within the security perimeter. To prevent unauthorized individuals from gaining access to the public side of the sports hall, a smartcard reader was installed at the entrance. Regarding the overall security of personnel, stricter checks were conducted at the gate and on protected interests. Due to the deterioration in relations with Russia, a Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (VJTF) unit was prepared within the framework of NATO for the entirety of 2017. In December, an alert exercise was held for this purpose, which will be further rolled out throughout 2017. In terms of support provision, both internally and to third parties, many activities were organized that aligned with previous years. This year also featured a family day, during which future relocation was also considered. For this purpose, the province of Zeeland and the municipality of Vlissingen were willing to contribute by providing information to the military personnel and their family members. In the context of the repurposing of the barracks area, in addition to many tours, other activities were also developed. Furthermore, the ongoing development of the needs for the new barracks in Vlissingen has once again required significant attention from several staff members of the barracks. Display of Medical Material.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.85)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance was officially transferred from DMO to CZSK with the unveiling of the nameplates Noordzee, Waddenzee, and Zuiderzee. Three captains (ktz) were fully trained and authorized to deploy the Noordzee-class for towing operations by mid-2016. The plan is for the two remaining captains to be fully trained by early 2017, resulting in five operational crews for the Noordzee-class from that point onward. In the months following the transfer, four tugboats of the Lingeklasse: Regge, Linge, Hunze, and Rotte, were decommissioned. The Gouwe is then the only remaining Lingeklasse tugboat that is part of the fleet. In addition to the fact that the operation of the Noordzee-class is very different compared to the Lingeklasse, the maintenance system was also significantly changed. This maintenance was structurally carried out at a civilian shipyard. The warranty period of the three boats has shown that civilian outsourcing of maintenance has so far yielded positive experiences. The second major theme within the product group was the optimization of operations. The goal was to facilitate the operational fleet as effectively as possible with the available resources. There was a continuous tension between the available personnel from the towing service and harbor watchmen (Steiger 19), various tasks, and a continuously fluctuating workload that is visible in the short term. The many ship-related activities such as dock planning, oil loading and unloading planning, ammunition loading and unloading planning, tours, practical lesson planning, responding to extreme weather conditions, and the deployment of tugboat crews posed a constant challenge for the Harbor Operations and Coordination Center (HOCC) and resulted in a dynamic planning process. The aim is to continue improving this process. In addition to coordinating and planning, active support was provided multiple times to the National Police, and civil-military cooperation with Port of Den Helder was continued. The Traffic Center (VTS) Den Helder registered more than 50,000 ship movements in 2016. The traffic management, which makes traffic decisions on behalf of the Rijkswaterstaat to ensure safe and smooth shipping movements, underwent several personnel changes, including the promotion of one of the former traffic managers to the position of Deputy Head of Traffic Service. Additionally, two candidates completed the training to become traffic managers; one of them is already a traffic manager, while the other will be ready early next year. The harbor watchmen (Steiger 19) played an essential role in the (un)mooring of ships. The small team, consisting of three employees in 2016, experienced a personnel change with the departure of a permanent staff member. Despite the highly fluctuating workload, the harbor watchmen made it possible for many vessels to enter the Waddenzee, the second tugboat of the new Noordzee-class, from Romania. Bridge of the Waddenzee.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.86)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance The Directorate of Material Maintenance carried out facilitating activities, allowing operations to continue uninterrupted. The bridge operators also experienced a personnel change and continue to operate the Vice Admiral Moorman Bridge with great enthusiasm. At the Central Quay Surveillance (CWB), the trend of recent years continued, with units being connected for longer periods of time. For more than two-thirds of the year, units made use of the CWB, significantly relieving ship crews from watch duties. Optimizing the operations of the CWB was an important point of focus. The work boats of the Schelde class, the multifunctional port vessels Nieuwediep, Marsdiep, and Landtdiep, the sailing/rowing boats (WR-1), and a variety of pontoons made it particularly challenging for the Kabelgat. In consultation with other parts of DMI, much effort was made to keep the availability of the vessels as high as possible. Despite many temporary personnel changes, where the formation of multiple shifts could proceed unhindered, the Kabelgat made a significant contribution to this. Product group energy distribution company Head: Ms. Drs. A.M. Valent-Groot The Energy Distribution Company has been the energy supplier and network manager for defense locations in Den Helder since 1957. With its own power plant, the Combined Heat and Power Station, electricity is generated, and the heat released is used to provide approximately half of the buildings at the Nieuwe Haven with warmth. Across the defense sector, the Energy Distribution Company manages contracts and invoice control for electricity, gas, and water. It also addresses demand requests and reports consumption figures, which are used to provide advice on reducing energy use. In 2016, it was 100 years since shore power was first supplied to a ship of the Royal Netherlands Navy in Den Helder. This means the Navy is far ahead of civil shipping, which has only recently begun to adopt shore power. With funds from the Van der Staaij Motion, a new employee for Integrated Safety and Quality was appointed at the EDB in April. This allowed for better compliance with safety, security, and environmental requirements within the EDB. In the same month, the assortment management of Energy and Water was formally transferred from the CDC to the EDB. The work had been carried out by the EDB since 2005. May 12 was a special day for the EDB. For the first time in 100 years of shore power, a ship returned power to the shore. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman had, in parallel with the KWS, supplied electricity to the EDB electricity grid. If necessary, the Karel Doorman can supply electricity to ships or to the shore, for example during maintenance of the generators on board or in exceptional circumstances, such as in aid to areas affected by a natural disaster. In June, the site lighting along the Koegraszeedijk was replaced with LED lighting. After the closing time of the Zuidpoort, the lighting is dimmed. Particularly, dimming contributes to energy savings compared to traditional site lighting. Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P.J. Baijards and project leader P.W. Terpstra took the first charging stations for electric cars into use.

Instead, the brass quintet of the band provided a successful alternative program at the Marine Museum in Rotterdam. The other outdoor performances took place under excellent sunny conditions. As early as 2015, a series of concerts had started together with trumpeter E. Vloeimans. These performances culminated in the live CD 'Around the World' and were presented on November 6 in Den Bosch during the presentation of the Prince Bernhard Culture Prize by the Commissioner of the King of North Brabant W. van de Donk to soloist Vloeimans. Several concerts were also conducted by guest conductors. For example, on January 23, a gala concert was held at Musis Sacrum in Arnhem under the direction of conductor A. Tien. Over eight hundred enthusiastic visitors enjoyed the band and the soloists P. Douwes and J. van der Boom. - Another conductor was Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P. Jansen, retired, at the National Tattoo in Rotterdam Ahoy.

sections.title: Jaarboek 2016 (p.88)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance performed at a grand anniversary concert on March 18 at the MECC Maastricht. On this evening, farewell was also given to the adjutants F. Klesman and H. Bertrand, two solo clarinetists who had both been permanent members of the Marine Band for over twenty-nine years. In September, conductor S. Teepen accompanied soloists drummer Cesar Zuiderwijk and trumpeter A. Heuvelman, and the annual Princess of Orange concert on December 7 at the Council of State in The Hague was conducted by I. Meylemans. Promising assistant conductor Sergeant F. Naval Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The naval training vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. The ship was specifically built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates sixteen trainees. In addition to the regular navigation bridge, the Van Kinsbergen has a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for safely practicing mooring and unmooring maneuvers and is equipped with a RHIB. Each year, the Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately 200 days. The main user is the KIM. The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, focusing on team building and character development. The ship is used as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. It is also deployed during the annual sailing period, during which a longer training voyage of about five weeks is undertaken together with a flotilla of minehunters; the cruise. Besides the KIM, the Operational School is also a major user. For this, practical sailing sessions are provided for the training of non-commissioned officers' sailing qualifications for minehunters. Marines also learn to operate landing craft with it. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Civil maritime schools also make good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Technical training on board is also possible. Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use the Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training trajectory. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO, universities) or for informational purposes. MOV Van Kinsbergen Jan-Dec For a few years now, the Van Kinsbergen has been sailing with a fixed schedule aligned with the Vocational Technical Education (VTO) periods. As a result, January of each year begins with the first sailing weeks for the beginning midshipmen on the Van Kinsbergen. The VTO period lasts a total of two years, during which these midshipmen undertake a sea service practicum (ZPR) on board the Van Kinsbergen three times for one week. The last ZPR lasts two weeks. The sailing week, together with a week on the Ship Handling Simulator (SHS), concludes a theoretical block. This allows for a progressive learning line to be realized, where the knowledge gained from the previous block serves as the basis for the subsequent block. This is also reflected in the program designed for the midshipmen. ZPR 1 is filled with the elementary aspects of navigation, such as learning to determine a position; evasive maneuvers; taking bearings; the operation of a 'leading line', and to break the week, a port visit. This is necessary to allow the midshipmen to process all the knowledge gained, but also to take a break; especially the night watch and the 24-hour operational concept can be quite challenging for most midshipmen. This is also the moment to provide the midshipman with summative feedback on their performance thus far. In 2015/2016, there was a transitional year. To better align the programs of both the KIM and the KMA, it was decided to conduct the VTO education for both the Long Officer Training (LOO) and the Short Officer Training (KOO) over one and a half years. This resulted in the LOO that started in 2014 still falling under the old arrangement and only beginning the VTO in the second year, while the new intake of 2015 also started the VTO education. Consequently, there was a 50 percent increase in students, workload, and sailing days for the first half of 2016. The four sailing weeks per block were therefore extended to six sailing weeks per block.

sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Training and Support A variety of exercises and training sessions took place in the Caribbean over the past year. This was to maintain the operational readiness of the own units, but also served as an ideal training location for CZSK, CLSK, and CLAS units or partners in the region. In addition to its own training, CZMCARIB also supported training of important strategic partners in the Caribbean, such as the United States and France. Units from CZMCARIB also trained abroad, for example at Camp Lejeune in Jacksonville, United States (Military Operations in Urban Terrain) and in French Guiana and Martinique (Unit Cohesion Training). The Fight Against Drugs Prompt action to ensure safety at sea and from the sea requires continuous vigilance. CZMCARIB is a '24/7 organization' where the Operations Center of the Maritime Headquarters Caribbean is staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. This results in operational successes each year. Over the past year, approximately 7000 kg of contraband was removed from the market, with Zr.Ms. Groningen having the largest 'catch' (2000 kg). Maritime Headquarters CARIB Head: kltz R.O.P. MHKC also frequently acted as the commander of military resources (CMM) for various military assistance requests from local authorities of the (island) countries in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in maintaining the international rule of law in the Caribbean. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy in the Caribbean is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization 'Joint Interagency Task Force South' based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization. Just before the summer leave, the Pelikaan once again provided transport for the CIDW to and from Bonaire. This transport was combined with support for a sniper training course from the Marine Training Center. Over several days, operational snipers from the Korps Mariniers and snipers in training were able to hone their skills in maritime sniping. After the summer leave, minor maintenance was carried out to ensure that all ship systems were functioning optimally again. This was immediately put to the test by supporting the visit of a unit from the United States Marine Corps Force Reconnaissance. In cooperation with the FRISC troop and other elements of the 32RSQN, the Pelikaan conducted amphibious training and practiced boat drills. The ship also served as a diving platform while logistical support was provided. 

On September 21, the transport of the CIDW from Bonaire was combined with a port visit and an open day. On this day, not only the Pelikaan visited the island, but also a cutter from the coast guard, the CURMIL, the KMar, and the CIDW were present during the open day. A large number of island residents, particularly several classes of elementary school students, visited the units and enjoyed the demonstrations. In the following week, a tropical disturbance developed over the Atlantic Ocean. This intensified to hurricane strength heading towards the Caribbean. Upon reaching the easternmost Caribbean islands, the forecast indicated that this hurricane Matthew would find its way to the Lesser Antilles. All units of the Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean prepared for a passage of the Lesser Antilles. Ultimately, Matthew passed as a Category 3 hurricane about two hundred miles north of the Lesser Antilles. The expected damage in Curaçao did not occur. Aruba and Bonaire particularly experienced extreme rainfall. 

On Monday, October 10, the Pelikaan departed with aid supplies, vehicles, and additional personnel towards heavily affected Haiti. The first stop was Aruba to pick up the marines from 32RSQN, along with extra supplies and vehicles. From October 10 to 30, the ship was deployed in close cooperation with marines from the 32RSQN to provide aid supplies to the most severely affected villages along the coast. The Pelikaan visited Port-au-Prince multiple times to take on aid supplies from various aid organizations. The crew members and marines then distributed the goods with the FRISC’s and carried out recovery projects in the affected villages. Government representatives and representatives from aid organizations were also on board to ensure that aid supplies reached the right places and could be distributed safely and in a coordinated manner. By the end of October, most communities had received emergency aid, and aid organizations took over the further structural rebuilding. The Pelikaan returned via Aruba to Curaçao for a week of leave. Due to the deployment in Haiti after the passage of Matthew, the planned transport weeks could not take place. However, there was a need for several goods in the Windward Islands. From November 14 to 22, the Pelikaan provided transport for these goods, including Super RHIBS for the coast guard. This week was combined with a port visit to San Juan, Puerto Rico, which partially coincided with the visit of the then-station ship Zr.Ms. Holland. Immediately after returning, Minister of Defense Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert visited Curaçao. On Wednesday, November 23, she presented several medals to crew members of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan for their efforts after the hurricane passage on the island of Dominica, one year earlier. After a week in port, the Pelikaan provided support from December 5 to 15 during the emergency aid operation in Haiti, moored next to Zr.Ms. Holland. Shelter boxes were ready on the helideck of the Holland.

Due to a reorganization at the Ministry of Education, the next trajectory (2017-1) has been canceled, leaving the future of SVT uncertain. The Green Platoon CURMIL The green platoon is the CURMIL unit that is actually operationally deployable. An important development for the platoon is that it falls under the MHKC as an operational unit. From here, the unit has been deployed for, among other things, manning observation posts. Additionally, the platoon has been on standby twice for deployment. The first time to support the KPC during potential unrest among striking Isla personnel. The second time because Hurricane Matthew was heading towards Curaçao. However, in both instances, actual deployment was not necessary. The General Service In addition to providing all different types of support to the various training programs, the SVT, the green platoon, and the permanent camp staff, there were also several visiting units at MKSUF this year. Some of these units and training programs now return annually, given the good facilities and local training areas. This effectively utilizes the facilitating role of MKSUF. In conclusion, 2016 has been a busy training year. An EMV, the VVO, pre-POTOC, and POTOC partially took place, and two SVTs were conducted. Additionally, units made use of the facilities of the barracks, especially in the autumn. Due to the involvement, commitment, and enthusiasm of the personnel, MKSUF was able to positively fulfill this role.
